summary: Blueprint for 'Algebraic topology of spaces and manifolds, Part II: homotopy foundations for algebraic K-theory' (RS-33). H.1 builds classifying spaces BC = |NC| from Mathlib's nerve and realisation, natural-transformation homotopies, contractibility, products, filtered colimits, coverings and π₁ via C[C⁻¹], local systems, homology of categories, BG as a K(G,1) and the bar/group-homology comparison. H.2 plans homotopy fibres and pullbacks with transport and the low-degree-correct long exact sequence, quasi-fibrations and the Dold–Lashof criteria, realisation of simplicial spaces (diagonal lemma, properness, levelwise equivalence and levelwise fibration theorems), Bousfield–Kan and Thomason homotopy colimits, and Quillen's Theorems A and B. H.3 plans acyclic maps, the plus construction (π₁, homology, acyclicity, universal property for abelian targets, uniqueness, functoriality, universal central extensions, relative forms), the obstruction theory for abelian spaces (K(G,n), representability, Postnikov towers, Hatcher 4.72–4.74), H-spaces, Serre classes and Cartan–Serre. H.4 plans S⁻¹S, Quillen's localisation theorem, group completions, cofinality and BGL⁺ comparisons, Segal's Γ-spaces and the Bhatt–Scholze E∞ model, and the hermitian applications of Calmès et al. H.5:spectra chooses symmetric spectra of simplicial sets (Schwede, Hovey–Shipley–Smith): homotopy groups, stable equivalences, the stable homotopy category as a triangulated category, smash product with its pairing and signs, ring and operadic algebra spectra, Eilenberg–Mac Lane spectra of groups, rings and chain complexes, cohomology representability, Postnikov sections, homotopy colimits and the comparison with deloopings and E∞-monoids. H.5:S-delooping assembles the K-theory symmetric spectrum from the deloopings of GeneralAlgebraicKTheory:K.4:construction. H.6 plans Moore spectra, coefficients, Bockstein and universal coefficient sequences, ℚ_p/ℤ_p coefficients, homotopy limits and the Milnor sequence, p-completion, rationalisation, the arithmetic square, filtered spectra, exact couples and their spectral sequences with convergence, the AHSS, and multiplicative Moore spectra. 170 nodes at lemma level.

nodes.title: Classifying space of a small category and of a functor
nodes.statement: For a small category C let BC = |NC| be the geometric realisation (Mathlib's SSet.toTop) of the nerve NC (Mathlib's CategoryTheory.nerve), whose p-simplices are strings X₀ → X₁ → ⋯ → X_p of composable morphisms, with i-th face deleting X_i (composing at interior positions) and i-th degeneracy inserting an identity. A functor F : C ⥤ D induces BF = |N F| : BC → BD, and B(G ∘ F) = BG ∘ BF, B(id) = id, so B is a functor Cat ⥤ TopCat (the composite SSet.toTop ∘ nerveFunctor).
hypotheses: C, D small categories (objects and morphisms in a fixed universe u), so that nerve C is an SSet.{u} and SSet.toTop applies.
No topology beyond Mathlib's TopCat is assumed; the compactly generated product enters only in H.1/classifying-space-prod.
proofSteps: Define classifyingSpace C := SSet.toTop.obj (nerve C) and classifyingSpaceMap F := SSet.toTop.map (nerveMap F); functoriality is that of the composite functor SSet.toTop ⋙ (nerveFunctor restricted to small categories) (Weibel IV Characterization 3.1(1), Definition 3.1.4).

The 0-cells are the objects of C and the 1-cells the non-identity morphisms; in general the n-cells are the strings of n composable non-identity morphisms (Recipe 3.1.1; the CW structure is the node H.1/classifying-space-cw-structure).

Remark (no proof obligation): for a poset P the nerve is the simplicial complex of finite chains (Quillen §1, LNM p. 89); for a group G viewed as a one-object category the construction gives BG (H.1/classifying-space-of-group).
acceptance: B(Fin (n+1)) for the ordered set 0 < ⋯ < n is the standard topological n-simplex (Weibel IV Characterization 3.1(2)).
B of the empty category is empty and B of the one-morphism category is a point (Weibel IV p. 24).
B of the one-object category with two morphisms 1, σ (σ² = 1) has one n-cell in each dimension and is RP^∞ (Weibel IV Example 3.1.2).

nodes.title: The realised boundary inclusion is the disk boundary inclusion
nodes.statement: For every n, the arrow SSet.toTop.map (∂Δ[n]).ι : |∂Δ[n]| ⟶ |Δ[n]| is isomorphic, in the arrow category of TopCat, to Mathlib's TopCat.diskBoundaryInclusion n : ∂𝔻 n ⟶ 𝔻 n. Combined with Mathlib's SSet.relativeCellComplex and the fact that realisation is a left adjoint, this makes |X| a TopCat.CWComplex (Mathlib's categorical CW complex) whose n-cells are the nondegenerate n-simplices of X.
hypotheses: n ≥ 0; Mathlib's conventions for 𝔻 n (closed unit ball of ℝⁿ) and ∂𝔻 n.
proofSteps: |Δ[n]| ≅ the topological simplex (mathlib:SimplexCategory.toTopHomeo).

∂Δ[n] is the union of the faces δᵢ. Realisation preserves this colimit, and the induced map from the colimit of the face simplices to the boundary of the topological simplex is a continuous bijection from a compact space to a Hausdorff one, hence a homeomorphism onto the boundary.
The simplex and its boundary are homeomorphic to (𝔻ⁿ, ∂𝔻ⁿ) by radial projection from the barycentre.
acceptance: n = 0: ∂Δ[0] is empty and 𝔻 0 is a point.
n = 1: |∂Δ[1]| is the two endpoints of |Δ[1]| ≅ [0,1] (Mathlib's SSet.stdSimplex.toTopObjIsoI).

nodes.title: The CW structure on the realisation of a simplicial set
nodes.statement: For a simplicial set X, the realisation |X| carries a CW structure (Mathlib's Topology.CWComplex) whose n-cells are indexed by the nondegenerate n-simplices of X, the characteristic map of x being the composite Δⁿ → |X| of the topological simplex with the image of x; a simplicial map induces a cellular map. For X = NC the n-cells are the strings of n composable non-identity morphisms, a subcategory C ⊆ D gives a subcomplex BC ⊆ BD, and B(⊔ C_α) = ⊔ BC_α.
hypotheses: X is any simplicial set (no finiteness); the topology on |X| is the weak (colimit) topology of Mathlib's SSet.toTop.
proofSteps: Mathlib's SSet.relativeCellComplex exhibits X as a relative cell complex for the boundary inclusions ∂Δ[n] → Δ[n], with one cell per nondegenerate simplex (Eilenberg–Zilber). Realisation is a left adjoint (sSetTopAdj), so it carries this to iterated pushouts in TopCat.

|∂Δ[n]| → |Δ[n]| is the disk boundary inclusion ∂𝔻ⁿ → 𝔻ⁿ (H.1/realisation-boundary-inclusion-disk), so |X| is a TopCat.CWComplex (Mathlib's categorical notion) with cells the nondegenerate simplices (Weibel IV Definition 3.1.4).

A categorical TopCat.CWComplex gives a classical Topology.CWComplex on its underlying space, with the same cells. This is a Mathlib TODO and is requested from Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 4, the owner of CW machinery under RS-33.
A simplicial map sends the n-skeleton to the n-skeleton, so its realisation is cellular; nondegenerate simplices of NC are strings with no identity arrow (Recipe 3.1.1).
acceptance: For C = Fin (n+1), |NC| has one top cell and is the n-simplex.
The 1-skeleton of BC is the graph with vertices objects and edges non-identity morphisms (used by H.1/maximal-tree-presentation).
Do not count degenerate simplices as cells: B of the one-morphism category has a single 0-cell and no higher cells.

nodes.title: B(C^op) is canonically homeomorphic to BC
nodes.statement: For a small category C there is a canonical cellular homeomorphism BC ≅ B(C^op), natural in functors F (B(F^op) corresponds to BF), sending each vertex to itself and the cell of a string X₀ → ⋯ → X_n to the cell of the reversed string in C^op by the order-reversing affine map of Δⁿ. It is not of the form BF for a functor F : C → C^op in general; for a group it is homotopic to, but not equal to, B of the isomorphism g ↦ g⁻¹.
hypotheses: C small.
proofSteps: The nerve of C^op is the simplicial set NC with faces and degeneracies reindexed by i ↦ n − i (the opposite simplicial set).

Realisation of the opposite simplicial set is naturally homeomorphic to the realisation, through the order-reversing affine maps of the simplices, compatible with faces after reindexing (Quillen §1 (3)). This is a general lemma about simplicial sets and a Mathlib TODO (SimplicialSet/Op.lean), as is nerve Cᵒᵖ ≅ (nerve C).op; split it off as SSet.toTopOpHomeomorph if it exceeds a page.
acceptance: For C = Fin 2 the homeomorphism is the reflection t ↦ 1 − t of the interval.

For a group G it is based-homotopic, not equal, to B of the isomorphism SingleObj G ≅ (SingleObj G)^op, g ↦ g⁻¹: the first sends the 1-cell of g to that cell traversed backwards, the second to the 1-cell of g⁻¹; both induce the same map on π₁ of these K(G, 1)s.

nodes.title: Classifying space of a product of categories
nodes.statement: For small categories C, D the projections induce a continuous bijection B(C × D) → BC × BD. If BD is a finite complex (nerve D has finitely many nondegenerate simplices), it is a homeomorphism onto the ordinary product; by symmetry the same holds when BC is finite. In particular B(C × Fin 2) ≅ BC × [0,1]. The compactly generated case for arbitrary C, D is H.1/classifying-space-prod-compactly-generated.
hypotheses: C, D small; nerve D finite (Mathlib's SSet.Finite).
proofSteps: On nerves, N(C × D) ≅ NC × ND (on simplices, a string in C × D is a pair of strings).

For standard simplices, |Δ[n] × Δ[m]| → Δⁿ × Δᵐ is a continuous bijection (staircase triangulation; Mathlib's SimplicialSet/ProdStdSimplex.lean lists the nondegenerate simplices) from a compact space to a Hausdorff one, hence a homeomorphism.

The inverse BC × BD → B(C × D) is continuous on each Δⁿ × Δᵐ. BC is a quotient of ⊔ Δⁿ (realisation is a colimit in TopCat), BD is a quotient of finitely many simplices, and Δⁿ and BD are locally compact. So Whitehead's lemma (mathlib:Topology.IsQuotientMap.continuous_lift_prod_left), applied in each variable, gives continuity on BC × BD.
acceptance: B(Fin 2 × Fin 2) is the square [0,1]² with its standard triangulation into two 2-simplices.

Without the finiteness hypothesis use the compactly generated product (H.1/classifying-space-prod-compactly-generated); if both factors have countably many cells the topologies agree (Hatcher Thm A.6).

sources.excerpt: is a homeomorphism if either BC or BC' is a finite complex
sources.match: Quillen's finite-complex case of (4); the compactly generated case is H.1/classifying-space-prod-compactly-generated.

nodes.title: Classifying space of a product, compactly generated case
nodes.statement: For arbitrary small categories C, D the canonical continuous bijection B(C × D) → BC × BD (induced by the projections) is a homeomorphism when BC × BD is given the compactly generated (k-ified) product topology. If C and D have countably many morphisms, the k-ification does not change the topology (Hatcher Thm A.6), so the map is a homeomorphism onto the ordinary product.
hypotheses: C, D small; the product on the right is formed in compactly generated spaces (no finiteness).
proofSteps: N(C × D) ≅ NC × ND (H.1/classifying-space-prod, step 1).
|K × L| ≅ |K| ×_k |L| for simplicial sets K, L, with the compactly generated product (Milnor 1957, imported by Quillen §1 (4); not read; gap 'Realisation of products').
acceptance: When BD is a finite complex this agrees with H.1/classifying-space-prod, because the k-ification of BC × BD is then the ordinary product.
B(S × S) → BS × BS for a symmetric monoidal S is the multiplication input of H.4/classifying-space-hspace.

sources.excerpt: and also if the product is given the compactly generated topology
sources.match: Quillen's (4), compactly generated case, citing Milnor.

nodes.title: A natural transformation induces a homotopy
nodes.statement: Let F₀, F₁ : C ⥤ D be functors between small categories and η : F₀ ⟶ F₁ a natural transformation. Then there is a homotopy H : BC × [0,1] → BD from BF₀ to BF₁, namely B of the functor C × Fin 2 ⥤ D determined by (F₀, F₁, η), composed with B(C × Fin 2) ≅ BC × [0,1]; on each vertex [X] its track is the edge path of η_X. Consequently functors related by a zig-zag of natural transformations induce homotopic maps. (The consequences for adjoints, equivalences and initial or terminal objects are the nodes H.1/adjunction-homotopy-equivalence and H.1/contractible-of-initial-or-terminal.)
hypotheses: C, D small; the identification B(C × Fin 2) ≅ BC × [0,1] is the finite-factor case H.1/classifying-space-prod, which needs no compactly generated spaces.
proofSteps: A natural transformation η : F₀ ⟶ F₁ is the same as a functor C × Fin 2 ⥤ D restricting to F_i on C × {i} (Quillen Prop. 2 proof).
Apply B and precompose with the inverse of B(C × Fin 2) → BC × B(Fin 2) = BC × [0,1], a homeomorphism because B(Fin 2) is finite (H.1/classifying-space-prod).
acceptance: The track of the homotopy at [X] is the edge classifyingSpace.edge (η.app X).
Comparable monotone maps f ≤ g : P → Q of posets give homotopic maps BP → BQ (the case of a preorder, used by ArithmeticKTheory:N.3).
A natural isomorphism gives a homotopy, but not a homotopy relative to a basepoint unless η is the identity there.

nodes.title: Adjoint functors and equivalences induce homotopy equivalences
nodes.statement: If L : C ⥤ D is left adjoint to R : D ⥤ C (small categories), then BL : BC → BD and BR : BD → BC are mutually inverse homotopy equivalences. In particular an equivalence of small categories induces a homotopy equivalence of classifying spaces, so B of a skeletally small category is well defined up to homotopy equivalence.
hypotheses: C, D small.
proofSteps: The unit id_C ⟶ R ∘ L and counit L ∘ R ⟶ id_D are natural transformations, so B(R ∘ L) ≃ id and B(L ∘ R) ≃ id (H.1/natural-transformations-adjoints-contractibility), and B(R ∘ L) = BR ∘ BL by functoriality (Quillen Prop. 2 Cor. 1).
An equivalence of categories has an adjoint inverse (Weibel IV Example 3.2.1).
acceptance: The inclusion of a skeleton into a skeletally small category is a homotopy equivalence of classifying spaces.
A functor with an adjoint is a homotopy equivalence even if it is not an equivalence of categories (e.g. C → 1 when C has a terminal object).

sources.excerpt: If a functor f has either a left or a right adjoint, then f is a homotopy equivalence.
sources.match: Quillen's Corollary 1 to Proposition 2.

sources.excerpt: Any equivalence C0 −→ C between small categories induces a homotopy equivalence BC0 −→ BC, because F has an adjoint.
sources.match: Weibel's adjoint consequence and the smallness remark.

nodes.title: Categories with an initial or terminal object are contractible
nodes.statement: A small category with an initial object or a terminal object has contractible classifying space.
hypotheses: C small and nonempty with an initial (or terminal) object.
proofSteps: If C has an initial object then the functor C → 1 to the one-morphism category has a left adjoint (the inclusion of the initial object), so BC ≃ B1 = point (H.1/adjunction-homotopy-equivalence; Quillen Prop. 2 Cor. 2).
D/d has the terminal object id_d (Weibel IV Example 3.2.2).
acceptance: The comma category C/d has terminal object id_d and is contractible.
An additive category has the zero object as initial object, so BA is contractible; the interesting space is B(iso A) (Weibel IV §4 opening).
The empty category has no initial object and B∅ = ∅ is not contractible.
For a functor F : C ⥤ D with right adjoint G and d in D, F/d has the terminal object (Gd, ε_d), so B(F/d) is contractible; dually d\F is contractible when F has a left adjoint (packet-authored).

sources.excerpt: A category having either an initial or a final object is contractible.
sources.match: Quillen's Corollary 2.

sources.excerpt: Any category with an initial object is con-tractible, because then the natural functor C → 1 has a left adjoint.
sources.match: Weibel's statement and its comma-category application.

nodes.title: The nerve commutes with filtered colimits of categories
nodes.statement: Let I be a filtered small category, F : I ⥤ Cat a functor and c a colimit cocone of F in Cat. Then nerveFunctor.mapCocone c is a colimit cocone in SSet; equivalently, for each n the n-simplices of nerve c.pt are the filtered colimit of the n-simplices of nerve (F i). In particular a simplicial subset of nerve c.pt with finitely many nondegenerate simplices is the image of a simplicial subset of some nerve (F i), and two such lifts agree after enlarging i.
hypotheses: I filtered (nonempty, cocones on pairs, coequalisers of parallel arrows); the colimit is taken in Cat.
proofSteps: Filtered colimits of sets commute with finite limits. The functors Ob and Ar : Cat → Set preserve filtered colimits: the colimit category has objects colim Ob(F i) and morphisms colim Ar(F i), with composition defined on representatives (Quillen §1, LNM p. 92).

The n-simplices of the nerve (Mathlib: ComposableArrows C n) form the finite limit Ar ×_Ob ⋯ ×_Ob Ar, so they commute with filtered colimits. Colimits in SSet are computed levelwise, so the image cocone is a colimit.
A finite simplicial subset is generated by finitely many simplices. Each comes from some F i; filteredness gives a common index and identifies the finitely many face relations.
acceptance: For the chain Fin 1 ⊂ Fin 2 ⊂ ⋯ with colimit the poset ℕ, every simplex of N(ℕ) lies in N(Fin k) for k beyond its top vertex.

Fails for non-filtered colimits: the pushout in Cat of 0 → 1 and 1 → 2 along the object 1 contains the composite 0 → 2 and a 2-simplex. The pushout of the nerves is the horn Λ[2,1], which has neither.

sources.excerpt: because filtered inductive limits commute with finite projective limits, we have ObC = lim ObC_i, ArC = lim ArC_i, and more generally NC = lim NC_i
sources.match: Quillen's statement of the lemma, used in the proof of Proposition 3.

nodes.title: Homotopy groups commute with filtered colimits of categories
nodes.statement: Let I be a filtered small category, i ↦ C_i a functor I ⥤ Cat with colimit C (computed in Cat), and choose compatible objects X_i of C_i with common image X. Then the canonical map colim_i π_n(BC_i, [X_i]) → π_n(BC, [X]) is a bijection for all n ≥ 0 (a group isomorphism for n ≥ 1), and π₀(BC) = colim_i π₀(BC_i).
hypotheses: I filtered (nonempty, every two objects have a common target, parallel arrows are coequalised).
The colimit is taken in Cat.
proofSteps: NC = colim_i NC_i levelwise (H.1/nerve-filtered-colimit); a simplicial subset with finitely many nondegenerate simplices lifts to some NC_i, uniquely after enlarging i (Quillen Prop. 3 proof).

Every compact subset of |NC| lies in the realisation of a finite simplicial subset, which is a closed subspace (API items SSet.toTop_isCompact_subset_finite_subcomplex and SSet.toTop_map_isClosedEmbedding_of_mono of H.1/classifying-space-cw-structure; Mathlib has no compactness lemma for CW complexes), so spheres and homotopies of spheres in BC lift to some BC_i; this gives surjectivity and injectivity of the colimit map.
acceptance: For the chain Fin 1 ⊂ Fin 2 ⊂ ⋯ with colimit the poset ℕ, π_n(Bℕ, [0]) = colim_k π_n(B(Fin k), [0]) = 0 for all n.
For GL(R) = colim GL_n(R): π_n(BGL(R)) = colim π_n(BGL_n(R)).

sources.excerpt: Let I be a small category which is filtering (= non-empty + directed [Bass, p.41]) and let i ↦ C_i be a functor from I to small categories.

nodes.title: Filtered colimits along homotopy equivalences
nodes.statement: In the situation of H.1/filtered-colimits-of-categories, if every transition functor C_i → C_{i'} is a homotopy equivalence then every C_i → C is a homotopy equivalence.
hypotheses: I filtered; transition functors homotopy equivalences.
proofSteps: Replace I by the cofinal category i\I, which has initial object id_i; each π_n(BC_i) → colim is then an isomorphism, the transition maps being bijective (tauceti:HomotopyGroup.map_bijective_of_homotopyEquiv), so BC_i → BC is a weak equivalence (H.1/filtered-colimits-of-categories).
A weak equivalence between CW complexes is a homotopy equivalence (Whitehead's theorem, Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 8).
acceptance: Do not apply when transition functors are not homotopy equivalences: the inclusions GL_n(R) → GL_{n+1}(R) are not homotopy equivalences of classifying spaces.

sources.excerpt: Suppose in addition that for every arrow i → i' in I the induced functor C_i → C_i', is a homotopy equivalence. Then the functor C_i → C is a homotopy equivalence for each i.
sources.match: Quillen's Corollary 1 to Proposition 3 (scan OCR; the hypothesis is that the transition functors are homotopy equivalences).

nodes.title: Filtered categories are contractible
nodes.statement: Every filtered small category I has contractible classifying space.
hypotheses: I filtered (in particular nonempty).
proofSteps: I is the filtered colimit of the functor i ↦ I/i, and each I/i has a terminal object, hence is contractible (H.1/contractible-of-initial-or-terminal).
The transition functors between contractible categories are homotopy equivalences, so BI ≃ B(I/i) ≃ point (H.1/filtered-colimit-homotopy-equivalence; Quillen Prop. 3 Cor. 2).
acceptance: A directed poset (ℕ with ≤) is contractible.
The discrete category on two objects is not filtered and B of it is two points.

sources.excerpt: Any filtering category is contractible.
sources.match: Quillen's Corollary 2.

nodes.title: Homology of classifying spaces commutes with filtered colimits
nodes.statement: For I filtered and C = colim_i C_i in Cat, and any abelian group A, the canonical map colim_i H_n(BC_i; A) → H_n(BC; A) is an isomorphism for every n, natural in the diagram. The same holds for the category homology H_n(C; M) of H.1/category-homology when M is the restriction of a functor on C.
hypotheses: I filtered; constant coefficients A, or coefficient functors restricted along C_i → C.
proofSteps: The normalised chain complex of NC is the filtered colimit of those of NC_i, since each nondegenerate simplex of NC lies in the image of some NC_i (H.1/nerve-filtered-colimit).

Filtered colimits of abelian groups are exact, so homology commutes with them; compare with singular homology through H.1/homology-of-small-categories (cellular chains of BC are normalised chains of NC).
acceptance: For the increasing rank-filtered subcategories Q_m of Q(P(A)), colim_m H_i(BQ_m; ℤ) ≅ H_i(BQ; ℤ) (the use in ArithmeticKTheory:N.3).
H_*(BGL(R)) = colim_n H_*(BGL_n(R)) (used in H.4/gl-telescope-plus-comparison).

nodes.title: Path components of a classifying space
nodes.statement: π₀(BC) is the quotient of the set of objects of C by the equivalence relation generated by X ∼ Y whenever there is a morphism X → Y, i.e. the set of connected components of C (Mathlib's ConnectedComponents C); BC is path-connected iff C is connected.
hypotheses: C small.
proofSteps: SSet.π₀ (nerve C) ≃ ConnectedComponents C: the edges of the nerve are the morphisms (combinatorial).

For any simplicial set X, ZerothHomotopy |X| ≃ SSet.π₀ X, sending ⟦vertex x⟧ to π₀.mk x. Every point is joined to a vertex inside a simplex (classifyingSpace_joined_vertex), and a path meets finitely many cells, so it is homotopic to an edge path (Weibel IV Lemma 3.3).
acceptance: For a G-set X, π₀ of the translation category is the orbit set X/G (Weibel IV 3.3.1).
π₀ of B(iso P(R)) is the set of isomorphism classes of finitely generated projective modules.
For the Grothendieck construction ∫_I X of X : I ⥤ Cat, π₀(B∫_I X) = colim_i π₀(BX(i)) (Weibel IV Example 3.3.2; a consequence of this node and Lemma 3.3, to be proved where used).

sources.excerpt: Let ∼ be the equivalence relation on obj(C) which is generated by the relation that c ∼ c′ if there is a morphism in C between c and c′ .
sources.match: Weibel's Lemma 3.3 with π0(C) = obj(C)/∼.

nodes.title: Realisations of simplicial coverings are covering maps
nodes.statement: Let p : E ⟶ X be a map of simplicial sets that is a simplicial covering: for every simplex σ : Δ[n] ⟶ X, the pullback of p along σ is isomorphic over Δ[n] to the projection Δ[n] × S_σ → Δ[n] for a set S_σ. Equivalently, every simplex of X has exactly one lift through each lift of its 0-th vertex. Then SSet.toTop.map p is a covering map (Mathlib IsCoveringMap) whose fibre over the vertex x is the set of 0-simplices of E over x.
hypotheses: p a simplicial covering in the sense above; no finiteness.
proofSteps: Over each simplex the realisation of the pullback is Δⁿ × S_σ with S_σ discrete: realisation preserves coproducts.

Local triviality uses neighbourhoods built from the weak topology, not unions of open cells, which are not open. In BG every cell has the single vertex in its closure. For a point in the open cell of a nondegenerate σ, take the union, over the simplices τ having σ as an iterated face, of the images of fixed open neighbourhoods of that face in Δ^{dim τ}. Unique lifting of simplices makes its inverse image a disjoint union of homeomorphic copies (Gabriel–Zisman, App. I, 3.2; not read; gap 'Gabriel–Zisman imports').
acceptance: N(ActionCategory G G) → N(SingleObj G) is a simplicial covering with fibre G, so EG → BG is a covering map.
Non-example: N(Fin 2) → Δ[0] is not a simplicial covering. The degenerate 1-simplex of Δ[0] has three lifts (two degenerate, one nondegenerate), and [0,1] → point is not a covering.

nodes.title: Coverings of BC are morphism-inverting functors
nodes.statement: For a small category C, the functor sending a covering space E → BC to X ↦ (fibre of E over the vertex [X]) is an equivalence between the category of covering spaces of BC and the category of morphism-inverting functors C ⥤ Type (those sending every morphism to a bijection), with inverse F ↦ (B(F.Elements) → BC), the realisation of the projection from the category of elements (Mathlib's Functor.Elements). Equivalently, morphism-inverting functors are functors C[C⁻¹] ⥤ Type from the localisation of C at all morphisms.
hypotheses: C small; covering spaces in Mathlib's sense (IsCoveringMap); BC is locally contractible, hence locally path-connected and semilocally simply connected (API item SSet.toTop_locallyContractibleSpace of H.1/classifying-space-cw-structure; tauceti:TauCeti.SemilocallySimplyConnectedSpace.of_locallyContractibleSpace).
proofSteps: Given a covering E → BC, path lifting along the edges classifyingSpace.edge f defines bijections E_[X] → E_[Y] functorial in f, so X ↦ E_[X] is morphism-inverting (Quillen §1, LNM p. 90).

Given F morphism-inverting, the projection F.Elements → C (Mathlib's Functor.Elements.π) realises to a map whose fibre over [X] is F(X); the projection N(F.Elements) → NC is a simplicial covering (its pullback along a string X₀ → ⋯ → X_n is Δ[n] × F(X₀), the transition maps being bijections), so its realisation is a covering map (H.1/simplicial-covering-realisation). Open cells are not open, so local triviality cannot be checked cell by cell (Quillen §1 cites Gabriel–Zisman App. I 3.2; Weibel IV Exercise 3.1).
The two constructions are inverse up to natural isomorphism by the unique path lifting property (Tau Ceti UniversalCovers stage 2 lifting and classification).
acceptance: For a group G, coverings of BG correspond to G-sets (Weibel IV 3.3.1 and Exercise 3.2).
For H ⊂ G the homotopy fibre of BH → BG is the discrete set G/H, while the strict fibre category of SingleObj H → SingleObj G is a point (Weibel IV Exercise 3.3).

nodes.title: π₁ of BC is the automorphism group in C[C⁻¹]
nodes.statement: For a small category C, the fundamental groupoid of BC restricted to the vertices is equivalent to the localisation C[C⁻¹] of C at all its morphisms (Mathlib's MorphismProperty.Localization at ⊤, or the free groupoid on C modulo composition), by the functor FreeGroupoid.lift classifyingSpace_edgeFunctor, sending X to [X] and f to the path class of classifyingSpace_edge f. Hence π₁(BC, [X]) ≅ Aut_{C[C⁻¹]}(X), naturally in functors C ⥤ D.
hypotheses: C small.
proofSteps: Every point of BC is joined to a vertex inside its open cell (classifyingSpace_joined_vertex), so the vertex-restricted fundamental groupoid is equivalent to the full one.

Morphism-inverting functors C ⥤ Type are functors C[C⁻¹] ⥤ Type (universal property of the localisation), and coverings of BC are functors from its fundamental groupoid to Type (Tau Ceti UniversalCovers stage 2); H.1/coverings-fundamental-group-local-coefficients identifies these two categories compatibly with fibre functors.

A functor between groupoids inducing an equivalence on categories of Type-valued functors compatible with evaluation at objects is an equivalence (Gabriel–Zisman I 1.2, not read; recorded as part of the packet gap 'Gabriel–Zisman imports').
acceptance: π₁(BG) = G for a group G (Weibel IV Application 3.4.1).
π₁(BM) is the group completion of the monoid M (Weibel IV Application 3.4.2).
For the poset ℕ, C[C⁻¹] is the indiscrete groupoid and π₁(Bℕ) = 1.

sources.excerpt: The fundamental group π₁(C,X) is canonically isomorphic to the group of automorphisms of X as an object of the groupoid G.
sources.match: Quillen's Proposition 1 (fundamental group); the groupoid form is the packet's strengthening, all points of BC being joined to vertices.

nodes.title: Presentation of π₁(BC) from a maximal tree
nodes.statement: Let C be a nonempty connected small category and T a maximal tree (a set of morphisms whose graph in the 1-skeleton of BC is a tree containing every object). Then π₁(BC, [c₀]) is generated by symbols [f], one for each morphism f of C, subject to [t] = 1 for t ∈ T, [id_X] = 1, and [f][g] = [f ∘ g] for composable f, g (in the order of the loop), the class of f : X → Y being the tree path from c₀ to X, the edge f, and the tree path back. The presentation does not depend on c₀.
hypotheses: C nonempty and connected; maximal trees exist by Zorn's lemma.
proofSteps: π₁(BC, [c₀]) ≅ Aut_{FreeGroupoid C}(c₀) (H.1/fundamental-groupoid-localization); the loop through f (tree path, edge f, tree path back) goes to the conjugate of [f] by the tree paths.

Mathlib's FreeGroupoid C is the free groupoid on the underlying quiver of C modulo [𝟙 X] = 1 and [f ≫ g] = [f][g]. In the free groupoid the vertex group at c₀ is free on the non-tree edges, via the tree paths (mathlib:IsFreeGroupoid.SpanningTree.endIsFree). Passing to the quotient imposes exactly [t] = 1 (t ∈ T), [id] = 1 and [f][g] = [f ∘ g] (Weibel IV Lemma 3.4).
acceptance: With T empty and C = SingleObj G, π₁(BG) = G.
For C = Fin 2 × Fin 2 (a commutative square) π₁ is trivial.

nodes.title: Local coefficient systems on BC are morphism-inverting functors
nodes.statement: For a small category C and a ring R, restriction along FreeGroupoid.lift classifyingSpace_edgeFunctor : C[C⁻¹] ⥤ FundamentalGroupoid BC (X ↦ [X], f ↦ [edge f]), is an equivalence between Tau Ceti's local coefficient systems of R-modules on BC (functors FundamentalGroupoid BC ⥤ ModuleCat R) and morphism-inverting functors C ⥤ ModuleCat R, compatible with pullback along BF for functors F : C ⥤ D and with constant systems.
hypotheses: C small; R a ring; morphism-inverting means every morphism goes to an isomorphism.
proofSteps: By H.1/fundamental-groupoid-localization the vertex fundamental groupoid of BC is equivalent to C[C⁻¹].
Functors C[C⁻¹] ⥤ ModuleCat R are exactly morphism-inverting functors C ⥤ ModuleCat R (universal property of localisation).
Compatibility with pullback follows from naturality of the localisation equivalence in C.
acceptance: A G-module M is a local system on BG (Weibel IV 3.5.1 and Application 3.4.2).
The constant system R corresponds to the constant functor; a non-morphism-inverting functor (for example X ↦ R on Fin 2 with the zero map) is not a local system.

nodes.title: Homology of a small category with coefficients in a functor
nodes.statement: For a small category C and a functor M : C ⥤ ModuleCat R, H_n(C; M) is the n-th homology of the chain complex C_*(C; M) with C_n = ⊕_{X₀ → ⋯ → X_n} M(X₀) (sum over n-simplices of NC) and boundary Σ (−1)^i d_i, where d₀ uses M(f₁) : M(X₀) → M(X₁) and the other faces are identities on the summand; equivalently the homology of the simplicial R-module n ↦ ⊕_{NC_n} M(X₀) (its alternating face map complex, or the normalised complex). H₀(C; M) = colim_C M.
hypotheses: C small, R a ring; no condition on M (it need not be morphism-inverting).
proofSteps: Build the simplicial module from NC and M (a coefficient system on the category of simplices), take Mathlib's alternatingFaceMapComplex, then homology (Weibel IV 3.5).
Normalised and unnormalised complexes are chain homotopy equivalent (Mathlib's Dold–Kan normalisation comparison), so either computes H_*(C; M).
Identify H₀ with the cokernel of ⊕_{X₀→X₁} M(X₀) → ⊕_X M(X), x ↦ (−x, fx), which is colim M (Weibel IV 3.5).
acceptance: H₀(C; M) = colim_{c∈C} M(c).
For C = SingleObj G and a G-module M this is the bar complex computing group homology (H.1/bar-complex-comparison).

nodes.title: Homology of a category computes derived functors of colim
nodes.statement: For a small category C and a ring R, the functors M ↦ H_n(C; M) on Fun(C, ModuleCat R) form a universal homological δ-functor with H₀ = colim, so H_n(C; M) ≅ L_n colim(M), the left derived functors of colim : Fun(C, ModuleCat R) → ModuleCat R.
hypotheses: C small, R a ring; Fun(C, ModuleCat R) has enough projectives (sums of representables R[C(X, −)]); this is a fact to prove, recorded in the gap 'Gabriel–Zisman imports', not an assumption.
proofSteps: H_*(C; −) is an exact δ-functor because the chain complex is exact in M (H.1/category-homology long exact sequence).

It is effaceable in positive degrees: for a representable projective R[C(X, −)] the simplicial module ⊕_{X → X₀ → ⋯ → X_n} R, augmented to R, has the extra degeneracy prepending 𝟙_X, so H_n = 0 for n > 0 and H₀ = R (mathlib:CategoryTheory.SimplicialObject.Augmented.ExtraDegeneracy.homotopyEquiv; Quillen §1, citing Gabriel–Zisman App. II 3.3).

An exact δ-functor agreeing with colim in degree 0 and effaceable in positive degrees is isomorphic to L_* colim, by dimension shifting along 0 → K → ⊕ R[C(X,−)] → M → 0. Neither library has δ-functors, nor EnoughProjectives for Fun(C, ModuleCat R); both are recorded in the gap 'Gabriel–Zisman imports'.
acceptance: For C with a terminal object, colim is evaluation at it and is exact, so H_n = 0 for n > 0.
For C = SingleObj G this recovers Tor^{ℤG}_n(ℤ, M).

nodes.title: Cellular chains of BC with local coefficients are the normalised chains of C
nodes.statement: Let C be a small category and L : C ⥤ ModuleCat R a morphism-inverting functor, regarded as a local system on BC (H.1/local-systems-as-functors). For each n, the twisted relative homology H_q(BC^{(n)}, BC^{(n−1)}; L) vanishes for q ≠ n and is isomorphic to ⊕ L(X₀) over the nondegenerate n-simplices X₀ → ⋯ → X_n for q = n. Under these isomorphisms the connecting map of the triple (BC^{(n)}, BC^{(n−1)}, BC^{(n−2)}) is the normalised differential Σ(−1)ⁱdᵢ of C_*(C; L), with d₀ acting through L(f₁) : L(X₀) → L(X₁). Hence the cellular chain complex of BC with coefficients in L is isomorphic to the normalised complex of H.1/category-homology.
hypotheses: C small; L morphism-inverting; twisted singular chains as planned in Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 2 item 6.
proofSteps: Excision and additivity for twisted relative homology reduce H_*(BC^{(n)}, BC^{(n−1)}; L) to ⊕_σ H_*(Δⁿ, ∂Δⁿ; σ*L) through the characteristic maps (H.1/classifying-space-cw-structure). Excision with local coefficients is part of the gap 'Cellular homology with local coefficients'.
σ*L is a local system on the contractible simplex, hence trivial. Trivialising at vertex 0 identifies it with L(X₀), so H_*(Δⁿ, ∂Δⁿ; σ*L) is L(X₀) in degree n only.

The connecting map sends the σ-summand to the alternating sum over the faces dᵢσ. For i ≥ 1 the face keeps vertex 0 and the trivialisation is unchanged. For i = 0 the new initial vertex is 1, and the change of trivialisation along the edge f₁ is L(f₁). Degenerate faces contribute zero.
acceptance: For constant L = A this is the identification of the cellular complex of |NC| with Mathlib's normalised simplicial chain complex (nerve C).normalizedChainComplex A.

For C = SingleObj G and L a G-module M, this is the normalised bar complex: 'The cellular chain complex used to form the homology of BG with coefficients in M is the same as the canonical chain complex' (Weibel IV p. 28).

sources.excerpt: This may be proved by filtering the CW complex BC by means of its skeleta and considering the associated spectral sequence.

nodes.title: Homology of BC with local coefficients is homology of C
nodes.statement: For a small category C and a morphism-inverting functor L : C ⥤ ModuleCat R, regarded as a local coefficient system on BC (H.1/local-systems-as-functors), there is an isomorphism H_n(BC; L) ≅ H_n(C; L) between singular homology of BC with local coefficients (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 2 twisted chains) and the homology of C with coefficients in L, natural in (C, L). For constant coefficients this is H_n(BC; A) ≅ H_n(C; A).
hypotheses: C small; L morphism-inverting (a local system); singular homology with local coefficients as planned in Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 2.
proofSteps: Filter BC by skeleta (H.1/classifying-space-cw-structure); the relative homology of consecutive skeleta with coefficients L is ⊕ over nondegenerate n-simplices of L(X₀) concentrated in degree n, so the skeletal spectral sequence has E¹_{p,q} = 0 for q ≠ 0 (Quillen §1, compare Segal 1968 §5.1, not read).

The E¹-row is the normalised complex of H.1/category-homology (H.1/cellular-chains-local-coefficients), so the spectral sequence degenerates and gives the isomorphism; the cellular–singular comparison with local coefficients is imported from Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 4 (cellular homology) and stage 2 (twisted chains); its local-coefficient form is recorded in the packet gap 'Cellular homology with local coefficients'.
Weibel IV 3.5.1 gives the same isomorphism citing [Wh, VI.4.8].
acceptance: H₁(BG; ℤ) ≅ G/[G, G] for a group G (H.1 stage test).
For a nontrivial G-module M, H₀(BG; M) is the coinvariants M_G, not M.

nodes.title: Classifying space of a discrete group
nodes.statement: For a group G, BG := B(SingleObj G), the classifying space of G viewed as a one-object category; its nerve has n-simplices the n-tuples (g₁, …, g_n) ∈ Gⁿ with d₀ dropping g₁, d_n dropping g_n and d_i (0 < i < n) replacing g_i, g_{i+1} by their composite g_i ≫ g_{i+1} = g_{i+1} g_i (Mathlib's SingleObj convention, SingleObj.comp_as_mul). A homomorphism φ : G → H induces Bφ : BG → BH, based at the unique vertex, functorially. BG is a connected CW complex with one vertex and one 1-cell for each nontrivial element of G.
hypotheses: G a group in universe u (the same definition applies to monoids).
proofSteps: Apply H.1/nerve-and-classifying-space to SingleObj G and to the functor SingleObj.mapHom φ (Weibel IV Example 3.1.3).
The nerve of SingleObj G is the bar construction (the quotient EG/G of Mathlib's simplicial G-set EG by the diagonal action), which is the identification recorded in H.1/bar-complex-comparison.
acceptance: Bℤ/2 = RP^∞ (Weibel IV Example 3.1.2).
B of the trivial group is a point.

nodes.title: Classifying spaces of translation categories
nodes.statement: For a group G acting on a set X, the translation category ∫_G X (Mathlib's ActionCategory G X: objects x ∈ X, morphisms g : x → gx) has B(∫_G X) homotopy equivalent to ⊔_{orbits} BG_x (stabilisers); for X = G/H, B(∫_G X) ≃ BH. For X = G with left translation, ∫_G G is an indiscrete groupoid, so B(∫_G G) is contractible, and B(∫_G G) → BG is the universal covering of BG.
hypotheses: G a group acting on a set X.
proofSteps: Each orbit is a connected component (H.1/pi0-classifying-space); within a component the inclusion of the full subcategory on one object x, which is SingleObj G_x, is an equivalence of categories, hence a homotopy equivalence (H.1/adjunction-homotopy-equivalence).

For X = G every object is initial (unique morphism between any two objects), so B(∫_G G) is contractible (H.1/contractible-of-initial-or-terminal); the projection ∫_G G → SingleObj G is the Grothendieck construction of the morphism-inverting functor G, so it realises to a covering (H.1/coverings-fundamental-group-local-coefficients) with contractible total space (Weibel IV Exercise 3.2).
acceptance: B(∫_G (G/H)) ≃ BH.
For the trivial action on a set X, B(∫_G X) ≃ X × BG.

nodes.title: BG is a K(G,1)
nodes.statement: For every group G, the space BG is an Eilenberg–Mac Lane space K(G, 1) in the sense of Tau Ceti (path-connected, π₁(BG) ≅ G and π_n(BG) = 0 for n ≥ 2), with the isomorphism π₁(BG, *) ≅ G sending the loop of g to g; a homomorphism φ : G → H induces φ on π₁. In particular TauCeti.IsEilenbergMacLaneSpaceOne G BG ⋆ holds for every group G.
hypotheses: G any group.
proofSteps: π₁(BG) ≅ G by H.1/maximal-tree-presentation with T empty (Weibel IV Application 3.4.1), naturally in G.

The universal cover is B(∫_G G), which is contractible (H.1/translation-category-classifying-space), so π_n(BG) ≅ π_n(B(∫_G G)) = 0 for n ≥ 2 (covering maps induce isomorphisms on π_n for n ≥ 2: tauceti:IsCoveringMap.homotopyGroupMulEquiv).
acceptance: π_n(Bℤ) = 0 for n ≥ 2 and Bℤ ≃ S¹.
B(G × H) ≃ BG × BH as K(G×H, 1) (Tau Ceti product stability of K(G,1)).

sources.excerpt: By Lemma 3.4 (with T empty) we see that π1 (BG) = G. In fact, πi (BG) = 0 for all i ≥ 2. (See Ex. 3.2.)
sources.match: Weibel's statement; Exercise 3.2 supplies the vanishing of higher homotopy groups via the universal cover.

nodes.title: Conjugate homomorphisms induce freely homotopic maps
nodes.statement: Let φ : G → H be a homomorphism and h ∈ H, and let φ^h(g) = h φ(g) h⁻¹. Then Bφ and Bφ^h : BG → BH are freely homotopic; the homotopy moves the basepoint around the loop of h, and on π₁ the two maps differ by conjugation by h. In particular an inner automorphism of G induces a map BG → BG freely homotopic to the identity.
hypotheses: G, H groups.
proofSteps: The morphism h : ★ → ★ of SingleObj H is a natural isomorphism SingleObj.mapHom φ ⟶ SingleObj.mapHom φ^h: with SingleObj.comp_as_mul, naturality reads h * φ(g) = φ^h(g) * h.

A natural transformation induces a homotopy (H.1/natural-transformations-adjoints-contractibility) whose track at the vertex is the loop of h (classifyingSpaceMap_edge); a free homotopy conjugates the induced maps on π₁ by its track (tauceti:TauCeti.homotopyGroupTransport_map, or Mathlib's FundamentalGroupoidFunctor.homotopicMapsNatIso).
acceptance: For G abelian and φ = id, conjugation acts trivially.
The free homotopy is not in general a based homotopy: on π₁ the maps differ by an inner automorphism.

nodes.title: The nerve of a group is the bar construction
nodes.statement: For a group G and a G-representation M over a commutative ring k, the chain complex C_*(SingleObj G; M) of H.1/category-homology is isomorphic, compatibly with differentials and naturally in (G, M), to Mathlib's inhomogeneous chain complex of G with coefficients in M (the bar complex), so H_n(SingleObj G; M) ≅ groupHomology M n; composed with H.1/homology-of-small-categories this gives H_n(BG; M) ≅ H_n(G; M), natural in G and M and compatible with groupHomology.π.
hypotheses: G a group, k a commutative ring, M : Rep k G; group homology as defined in Mathlib by inhomogeneous chains.
proofSteps: An n-simplex of N(SingleObj G) is (g₁, …, g_n) and the summand M(X₀) is M; d₀(g; m) = (g₂, …, g_n; ρ(g₁)m), dᵢ replaces g_i, g_{i+1} by g_{i+1}g_i (SingleObj.comp_as_mul), d_n drops g_n (Weibel IV 3.4.2 and 3.5).

The maps ⊕_{Gⁿ} M → (Fin n → G) →₀ M, (g; m) ↦ single (fun i ↦ (g i)⁻¹) m, form an isomorphism of chain complexes categoryChainComplex k M ≅ groupHomology.inhomogeneousChains A, natural in (G, A). The check uses inhomogeneousChains.d_single: ρ((g₁⁻¹)⁻¹) = ρ(g₁), (g_{i+1}g_i)⁻¹ = g_i⁻¹g_{i+1}⁻¹, and the signs (−1)ⁱ agree. Reversing the order of the entries would not give a chain map.
Naturality in G holds on the nose for the chain isomorphism; naturality of the homology isomorphism with respect to groupHomology.map and compatibility with groupHomology.π follow.
acceptance: H₁(BG; ℤ) ≅ G/[G, G] (Weibel IV p. 28).
For G = ℤ/n and trivial ℤ coefficients, H_{2i−1}(BG; ℤ) ≅ ℤ/n and H_{2i}(BG; ℤ) = 0 for i ≥ 1.

nodes.title: The nerve of a groupoid is a Kan complex
nodes.statement: If C is a small groupoid then nerve C is a Kan complex (Mathlib's SSet.KanComplex).
hypotheses: C a small groupoid.
proofSteps: n ≥ 4: every horn Λ[n, k] contains the 2-skeleton of Δ[n], since each 2-face lies in at least two (n−1)-faces other than the k-th. Nerves are 2-coskeletal (mathlib:CategoryTheory.Nerve.cosk₂Iso), so the horn extends uniquely.
n = 2: inner horns are filled by composition (Mathlib: nerve C is a quasicategory, CategoryTheory.Nerve.quasicategory). The outer horns Λ[2,0] and Λ[2,2] are filled with g ∘ f⁻¹ and f⁻¹ ∘ g.

n = 3: the horn determines all edges, and the missing 2-face commutes because the other three do and the arrows are invertible (for the missing d₀, cancel f₀₁ on the right). Then 2-coskeletality gives the 3-simplex. n = 1 is trivial.
acceptance: Non-example: nerve (Fin 2) is not Kan. The horn Λ[2,0] with edges 0→1 and 0→0 has no filler, since there is no morphism 1 → 0.
nerve (SingleObj G) is Kan for every group G.

nodes.title: Classifying spaces of groupoids are 1-types
nodes.statement: If C is a small groupoid, BC has π₀(BC) = isomorphism classes of objects, π₁(BC, [X]) ≅ Aut(X) and π_n(BC) = 0 for n ≥ 2, and BC is homotopy equivalent to ⊔_{[X] ∈ C/≅} B Aut(X). In particular B(Core S) ≃ ⊔ B Aut(s) for any category S.
hypotheses: C a small groupoid (all morphisms invertible).
proofSteps: The inclusion of the full subcategory on a set of representatives of isomorphism classes is an equivalence of categories, hence a homotopy equivalence (H.1/adjunction-homotopy-equivalence); that subcategory is ⊔ SingleObj Aut(X), B of a disjoint union is the disjoint union (H.1/classifying-space-cw-structure), and each B Aut(X) is a K(Aut X, 1) (H.1/classifying-space-of-group-is-KG1).
acceptance: For the groupoid of finite sets and bijections, B ≃ ⊔_n BΣ_n (Weibel IV Example 4.1.1(a)).
For a non-groupoid such as Fin 2 the nerve is not Kan.

nodes.title: Weak homotopy equivalences of spaces
nodes.statement: A continuous map f : X → Y is a weak homotopy equivalence if it induces a bijection π₀(X) → π₀(Y) and, for every x ∈ X and n ≥ 1, an isomorphism π_n(X, x) → π_n(Y, f x) (Mathlib's cubical homotopy groups, Tau Ceti's induced maps HomotopyGroup.mapHom). Weak homotopy equivalences satisfy two-out-of-three and contain homotopy equivalences; between CW complexes (more generally spaces of CW homotopy type) they are homotopy equivalences by Whitehead's theorem, imported from Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 8.
hypotheses: X, Y arbitrary topological spaces; all basepoints, not one.
proofSteps: Define the predicate from the bijection on π₀ and the isomorphisms on π_n at every basepoint (Hatcher §4.1, before Theorem 4.5).

Two-out-of-three and invariance under homotopy follow from functoriality of HomotopyGroup.mapHom and homotopy invariance of induced maps (Tau Ceti HomotopyGroup.map_eq_of_homotopicRel with basepoint transport).
acceptance: A homotopy equivalence is a weak homotopy equivalence.
The inclusion of a point in the Warsaw circle is a weak homotopy equivalence that is not a homotopy equivalence; Whitehead's theorem needs CW hypotheses.

nodes.title: Homotopy fibre of a map
nodes.statement: For a continuous map f : A → B and b ∈ B, the homotopy fibre F(f, b) is the subspace of A × C(I, B) (compact-open topology) of pairs (a, γ) with γ(0) = f(a) and γ(1) = b; it is pointed by (a₀, const) when f(a₀) = b, and comes with the projection F(f, b) → A, (a, γ) ↦ a. The strict fibre f⁻¹(b) includes as the pairs with constant γ. Convention pinned: paths run from f(a) to b (Quillen, Hatcher); Weibel's F(f) uses paths from the basepoint to f(e), and reversing paths is a natural homeomorphism between the two. A sequence F → A → B with F → B constant is a homotopy fibre sequence when the evident map F → F(f, b) is a weak homotopy equivalence.
hypotheses: f continuous; no fibration hypothesis; b any point of B.
proofSteps: Define homotopyFiber f b as the pullback of A × C(I,B) along evaluation at 0 and 1 (Hatcher §4.3 'Pathspace constructions', the fibre of E_f → B).
A commutative square (f′ : A′ → B′, f : A → B, α : A′ → A, β : B′ → B) with β(b′) = b induces F(f′, b′) → F(f, b), (a, γ) ↦ (α a, β ∘ γ), functorially.
The relation to Weibel's convention is the homeomorphism (a, γ) ↦ (a, γ reversed) (Weibel IV 1.2).
acceptance: For the inclusion of a point {b} → B, F = ΩB, the loop space at b (Hatcher p. 408).
For H ⊂ G the homotopy fibre of BH → BG is the discrete set G/H while the strict fibre category is a point (Weibel IV Exercise 3.3).
Record whether each low-degree homotopy set is a pointed set or a group (H.2/long-exact-sequence).

nodes.title: Every map factors through a fibration
nodes.statement: For f : A → B, the mapping path space E_f = {(a, γ) : γ(0) = f(a)} ⊂ A × C(I, B) with p(a, γ) = γ(1) is a Hurewicz fibration (homotopy lifting for all spaces), hence a Serre fibration in the sense of Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 5; the inclusion A → E_f, a ↦ (a, const), is a homotopy equivalence (E_f deformation retracts onto A) with p ∘ incl = f; the fibre of p over b is homotopyFiber f b.
hypotheses: f continuous; I = [0,1] with the compact-open topology on C(I, B), which is exponential because I is locally compact.
proofSteps: Lift a homotopy g_t : X → B with initial lift x ↦ (h x, γ_x) by g̃_t(x) = (h x, γ_x followed by g|[0,t](x)); continuity by the exponential law for C(I, B) (Hatcher Prop. 4.64).
Truncating paths to initial segments deformation retracts E_f onto A (Hatcher p. 407).
acceptance: For f a fibration the inclusion E ↪ E_p is a fibre homotopy equivalence (H.2/fibre-to-homotopy-fibre).
For f the inclusion of a point, E_f is the based path space PB, which is contractible.

nodes.title: Serre fibrations induce bijections on relative homotopy groups
nodes.statement: Let p : E → B have the homotopy lifting property for all discs D^k, k ≥ 0 (the Serre-fibration carrier of Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 5), b ∈ B, F = p⁻¹(b) and x₀ ∈ F. Then p_* : π_n(E, F, x₀) → π_n(B, b) is bijective for every n ≥ 1: a group isomorphism for n ≥ 2 and a bijection of pointed sets for n = 1.

nodes.title: Long exact sequence of a homotopy fibre
nodes.statement: For f : A → B and a₀ ∈ A with f(a₀) = b, write F = F(f, b) pointed at ā₀ = (a₀, const). The sequence ⋯ → π_{n+1}(B, b) →∂ π_n(F, ā₀) → π_n(A, a₀) → π_n(B, b) →∂ ⋯ → π₁(B, b) →∂ π₀(F) → π₀(A) → π₀(B) is exact: exactness at each term means image = kernel (preimage of the base point for pointed sets). The terms π_n are abelian groups for n ≥ 2, groups for n = 1 and pointed sets for n = 0, and the maps are homomorphisms where both sides are groups. The sequence is natural in commutative squares.
hypotheses: a₀ with f(a₀) = b; no fibration hypothesis on f (the homotopy fibre makes it one up to homotopy).
proofSteps: Replace f by the fibration E_f → B with fibre F (H.2/mapping-path-space-fibration); A ≃ E_f.

Apply H.2/fibration-relative-homotopy-iso to E_f → B: p_* : π_n(E_f, F, x₀) → π_n(B, b) is bijective for n ≥ 1 (relative groups of the arbitrary based pair (E_f, F) from Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 8).

Splice with the long exact sequence of the based pair (E, F) (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 8 item 1), identify the resulting boundary with H.2/connecting-map, and check exactness at π₀(F), π₀(A) directly.

nodes.title: The π₁-action at the pointed-set end of the fibre sequence
nodes.statement: For f : A → B with f(a₀) = b and F = F(f, b), the group π₁(B, b) acts on the set π₀(F) by transporting the path coordinate (concatenation with loops at b); the connecting map ∂ : π₁(B, b) → π₀(F) is the orbit map of the base point. Two elements of π₀(F) have the same image in π₀(A) iff they lie in the same π₁(B, b)-orbit, and the stabiliser of [ā₀] is the image of π₁(A, a₀) → π₁(B, b).
hypotheses: a₀ with f(a₀) = b.
proofSteps: Define the action by (a, γ) · ω = (a, γ · ω) for ω a loop at b; it respects homotopy classes.

If (a, γ), (a′, γ′) have path-connected images in A, a path from a to a′ transports γ to a path γ″ from f(a′) to b, and γ″⁻¹ · γ′ is a loop ω with (a′, γ″) · ω = (a′, γ′); conversely an orbit maps to one component.
The stabiliser computation is the exactness at π₁(B) of H.2/long-exact-sequence.
acceptance: For BH → BG with H ⊂ G a subgroup, π₀F = G/H with π₁(BG) = G acting by left translation; the stabiliser of the coset H is H = image of π₁(BH).

nodes.title: Transport of homotopy fibres along paths in the base
nodes.statement: For f : A → B and a path ω from b to b′ in B, transport T_ω : F(f, b) → F(f, b′), (a, γ) ↦ (a, γ · ω), is a homotopy equivalence with homotopy inverse T_{ω⁻¹}; its homotopy class depends only on the path class of ω, T_{const} ≃ id and T_{ω·ω′} ≃ T_{ω′} ∘ T_ω, so b ↦ F(f, b) is a functor from the fundamental groupoid of B to the homotopy category of spaces. Transport commutes with the projections to A and intertwines the connecting maps with Tau Ceti's change-of-basepoint isomorphisms on π_*(B), after the basepoint change inside F(f, b′) along t ↦ (σ t, ω|[t,1]) for a path σ in A with f ∘ σ = ω.
hypotheses: f continuous; ω a path in B.
proofSteps: Concatenation of paths is continuous on the path spaces (compact-open topology) and associative and unital up to homotopy rel endpoints (Mathlib Path.Homotopy).
A homotopy of paths ω ≃ ω′ rel endpoints gives a homotopy T_ω ≃ T_{ω′} by concatenating with the intermediate paths (Hatcher Prop. 4.61 proof, for the fibration E_f → B).
Compatibility with ∂ uses the definition of ∂ through ΩB and the basepoint change TauCeti.homotopyGroupMulEquivOfPath.
acceptance: For a constant loop ω, T_ω is homotopic to the identity.
For the inclusion of a point, transport along a loop ω acts on ΩB by right concatenation.

nodes.title: Homotopy pullbacks and homotopy-cartesian squares
nodes.statement: For maps f : A → B and g : C → B, the homotopy pullback A ×ʰ_B C is the space of triples (a, γ, c) with γ a path from f(a) to g(c). A commutative square with E′ → E over h : B′ → B (maps p′ : E′ → B′, p : E → B, α : E′ → E, p ∘ α = h ∘ p′) is homotopy-cartesian if the canonical map E′ → B′ ×ʰ_B E, e′ ↦ (p′ e′, const, α e′), is a weak homotopy equivalence. Quillen uses homotopy equivalence; the two agree for spaces of CW homotopy type (Whitehead), and the node fixes weak homotopy equivalence as the definition.
hypotheses: Maps of topological spaces; the square commutes strictly.
proofSteps: Define the homotopy pullback as the pullback of A × C(I, B) × C along evaluations (Quillen §1, LNM p. 96).
The homotopy fibre is the homotopy pullback along the inclusion of a point: F(f, b) = A ×ʰ_B {b}.

IsHomotopyCartesian.of_serreFibration: both E′ = B′ ×_B E → B′ and B′ ×ʰ_B E → B′ are Serre fibrations (AT stage 5 pullback; H.2/mapping-path-space-fibration); the comparison is the identity on bases and on fibres the inclusion p⁻¹(h b′) → F(p, h b′) of H.2/fibre-to-homotopy-fibre; conclude by H.2/long-exact-sequence and H.2/fibre-sequence-low-degree at every basepoint.
acceptance: A pullback square of a Serre fibration is homotopy-cartesian.
The square with the strict fibre of BH → BG is not homotopy-cartesian for H ≠ G.

nodes.title: Pasting homotopy-cartesian squares
nodes.statement: Given two adjacent commutative squares, (1) on the left and (2) on the right, with (2) homotopy-cartesian, the composite square (1)+(2) is homotopy-cartesian iff (1) is. Also, a square whose two horizontal maps are weak homotopy equivalences is homotopy-cartesian, and a square is homotopy-cartesian iff its transpose is (reverse paths, homotopyPullback.symm), so the pasting statement holds equally for vertically stacked squares, as used in Quillen's proof of Theorem B.
hypotheses: Squares commute strictly; weak homotopy equivalence as the comparison notion.
proofSteps: The homotopy pullback along a composite is the iterated homotopy pullback up to natural homotopy equivalence (concatenate paths), so the comparison maps factor through each other.
Apply two-out-of-three (H.2/weak-homotopy-equivalence); for horizontal equivalences compare homotopy fibres by H.2/long-exact-sequence and the five lemma.
acceptance: Used in the final step of the proof of Theorem B: (1)+(3) and (3) homotopy-cartesian imply (1) homotopy-cartesian (Quillen p. 99).

nodes.title: From comma categories to homotopy fibres
nodes.statement: For a functor f : C ⥤ C′ and an object Y of C′, the forgetful functor j : Y\f → C (objects (X, v : Y → fX)) and the natural transformation from the constant functor at Y to f ∘ j given by v induce a null-homotopy of B(f ∘ j) to the vertex [Y], hence a canonical map B(Y\f) → F(Bf, [Y]) (after reversing paths to the pinned convention), natural in Y for the transition functors u* : Y′\f → Y\f. Dually for f/Y.
hypotheses: f a functor between small categories; Y an object of C′.
proofSteps: The transformation (X, v) ↦ v : Y ⟶ f X gives a homotopy from the constant map at [Y] to B(f ∘ j) (H.1/natural-transformations-adjoints-contractibility), i.e. a map B(Y\f) → homotopyFiber (Bf) [Y] (Quillen §1, LNM p. 96; Weibel IV Example 3.2.3).
Naturality in u : Y → Y′ follows from the compatibility of the homotopies with u*.
acceptance: If f = id, the map B(Y\C′) → F(id, [Y]) is a map between contractible spaces.

nodes.title: Quasi-fibrations
nodes.statement: A continuous map p : E → B is a quasi-fibration if for every b ∈ B the inclusion of the strict fibre p⁻¹(b) into the homotopy fibre F(p, b) is a weak homotopy equivalence; equivalently (B path-connected) p_* : π_i(E, p⁻¹(b), x₀) → π_i(B, b) is bijective for all b, x₀ ∈ p⁻¹(b), i ≥ 0. Serre fibrations are quasi-fibrations; a quasi-fibration has the long exact sequence of its strict fibres.
hypotheses: p continuous; the definition quantifies over all points b of B.
proofSteps: Define the predicate through H.2/homotopy-fibre-and-long-exact-sequence and H.2/weak-homotopy-equivalence (Hatcher §4.K, alternative condition).
Equivalence with the relative-homotopy formulation: the triangle p⁻¹(b) → F_b → E_p with E ≃ E_p and the long exact sequence of the based pair (Hatcher p. 479).

nodes.title: Relative homotopy groups of excisive triads
nodes.statement: Let f : (X; A, B) → (Y; C, D) be a map of excisive triads (X is the union of the interiors of A and B, and likewise Y of C and D). If π_i(A, A ∩ B) → π_i(C, C ∩ D) and π_i(B, A ∩ B) → π_i(D, C ∩ D) are bijective for i < n and surjective for i = n, for all basepoints, then the same holds for π_i(X, A) → π_i(Y, C) (and by symmetry for π_i(X, B) → π_i(Y, D)).
hypotheses: Excisive triads; relative homotopy groups of arbitrary based pairs (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 8, as amended in the request).
proofSteps: Reduce to an inclusion of triads by the modified mapping cylinder of Hatcher p. 477-478 (enlarging M_f|A by f⁻¹(C) × (1/2, 1)).
For an inclusion (X, A) ⊆ (Y, C), bijectivity below n and surjectivity at n are equivalent to the extension conditions (ii) and (iii) for (D^n × I, ∂₋D^n × I) (Hatcher p. 477).
Subdivide I^n so that each subcube maps into C or D (Lebesgue number of the excisive cover) and extend over the subcubes by induction, keeping property (∗) of Hatcher p. 478.
acceptance: Hatcher Corollary 4K.2: a map carrying an open cover to an open cover and restricting to weak equivalences on all finite intersections is a weak equivalence.
The hypothesis on π_i(A, A ∩ B) cannot be dropped: the quotient D² → S² collapsing ∂D² to a pole, with C, D the hemispheres (Hatcher p. 476).

nodes.title: Dold–Lashof criterion for open covers
nodes.statement: A map p : E → B is a quasi-fibration if B = V₁ ∪ V₂ with V₁, V₂ open and the restrictions of p over V₁, V₂ and V₁ ∩ V₂ are quasi-fibrations. Criteria (b) and (c) of Hatcher Lemma 4K.3 are H.2/dold-lashof-exhaustion and H.2/dold-lashof-deformation.
hypotheses: As stated; B = V₁ ∪ V₂ with V₁, V₂ open. Hatcher proves the criterion only when all fibres are path-connected and leaves the general case as an exercise; Quillen's application (diagrams over a nerve whose spaces need not be connected) needs the general case of Dold–Lashof 1959, Lemmas 1.3–1.5 (not read).
proofSteps: For path-connected fibres: the five lemma for the triples (U_k, U₁ ∩ U₂, p⁻¹(b)) and (V_k, V₁ ∩ V₂, b), then H.2/excisive-triad-homotopy-comparison for π_i(E, U_k) → π_i(B, V_k), then the five lemma again (Hatcher Lemma 4K.3(a) proof).
The general case without connectivity of fibres is imported from Dold–Lashof 1959 Lemma 1.4 (gap: 'Dold–Lashof criteria for disconnected fibres').
acceptance: Over the open p-cells and their complement of barycentres it reduces H.2/quasi-fibration-lemma to the pieces U, V, U ∩ V.
Do not use it for disconnected fibres before the general case is supplied.

sources.match: Hatcher's Lemma 4K.3, conditions (a)–(c).

nodes.title: Dold–Lashof criterion for exhaustions
nodes.statement: If B is the union of an increasing sequence B₁ ⊆ B₂ ⊆ ⋯ such that every compact subset of B lies in some B_n, and each restriction p⁻¹(B_n) → B_n is a quasi-fibration, then p : E → B is a quasi-fibration.
hypotheses: Every compact subset of B lies in some B_n.
proofSteps: Compact subsets of E lie in some E_n = p⁻¹(B_n), and compact families of paths lie in some B_n, so homotopy groups of E, B, the strict fibres and the homotopy fibres are colimits of those over B_n (Hatcher p. 480, proof of (b)); take b ∈ B_n for n large.
The colimit of the weak equivalences p⁻¹(b) → F(p|E_n, b) is p⁻¹(b) → F(p, b).
acceptance: The skeletal filtration of a classifying space BI (compact subsets of a CW complex lie in finite skeleta) is the case used by H.2/quasi-fibration-lemma.

sources.excerpt: B is the union of an increasing sequence of subspaces B1 ⊂ B2 ⊂ ··· with the property that each compact set in B lies in some Bn
sources.match: Hatcher's criterion (b) (Dold–Lashof Lemma 1.5, as Quillen cites it).

nodes.title: Dold–Lashof criterion for deformations
nodes.statement: Suppose D_t is a deformation of E into a subspace E′ covering a deformation D̄_t of B into B′ (deformations in the weak sense: D₀ = id, D₁(E) ⊆ E′, D_t(E′) ⊆ E′, likewise for D̄, and p D_t = D̄_t p), that E′ → B′ is a quasi-fibration, and that D₁ : p⁻¹(b) → p⁻¹(D̄₁(b)) is a weak homotopy equivalence for every b ∈ B. Then p is a quasi-fibration.
hypotheses: Deformations in the weak sense (Hatcher p. 480).
proofSteps: D₁ : E → E′ and D̄₁ : B → B′ are homotopy equivalences; compare (E, p⁻¹(b)) → (E′, p⁻¹(D̄₁ b)) and (B, b) → (B′, D̄₁ b) by the five lemma on the long exact sequences of the pairs, using the hypothesis on fibres (Hatcher pp. 480-481, proof of (c)).
acceptance: H.2/quasi-fibration-lemma applies it with the radial deformation of Δᵖ minus its barycentre onto ∂Δᵖ.
The mapping-cylinder projection M_f → I deforms onto the end Y ⊆ M_f over {1}; when f is a weak equivalence the fibre maps are weak equivalences.

nodes.title: Realisation of simplicial spaces and bisimplicial sets
nodes.statement: For a simplicial space X : SimplexCategoryᵒᵖ ⥤ TopCat, the realisation |X| is the coend ∫ⁿ X_n × Δⁿ (quotient of ⊔ X_n × Δⁿ by the face and degeneracy identifications), functorial in X. For a bisimplicial set T (a simplicial object in SSet, T_{p,q}) define |T| = |p ↦ |T_{p,•}|| (realise in q, then in p); for a levelwise discrete simplicial space this is Mathlib's SSet.toTop. Realisation is a left adjoint (to Y ↦ (n ↦ C(Δⁿ, Y))), hence preserves colimits.
hypotheses: X any simplicial object in TopCat; the coend is formed in TopCat (Mathlib's colimits).
proofSteps: Define |X| as a coend (or a colimit over the category of simplices) in TopCat; its right adjoint is the singular simplicial space (Quillen §1, Lemma hypothesis).
For X levelwise discrete, |X| agrees with SSet.toTop of the underlying simplicial set by the coend formula defining SSet.toTop (left Kan extension of the topological simplex).
For a bisimplicial set, the realisation of a product of representables Δ[r] ⊠ Δ[s] is Δ^r × Δ^s (H.1/classifying-space-prod with finite factors).
acceptance: The realisation of the constant simplicial space at Y is Y.
|Δ[r] ⊠ Δ[s]| = Δ^r × Δ^s (Weibel IV 3.10.1).

nodes.title: Realisation of bisimplicial spaces: diagonal and iterated realisations agree
nodes.statement: For a bisimplicial space T, realising first in q then in p, first in p then in q, and realising the diagonal simplicial space p ↦ T_{p,p} give spaces related by homeomorphisms functorial in T. In particular the realisation of a bisimplicial set is homeomorphic to the realisation of its diagonal simplicial set.
hypotheses: Realisation of simplicial spaces is the left adjoint of H.2/simplicial-space-realisation, so it commutes with colimits.
The representable case uses the product homeomorphism |Δ[r] × Δ[s]| ≅ Δ^r × Δ^s (finite complexes, H.1/classifying-space-prod).
proofSteps: Check the three realisations agree functorially on bisimplicial spaces of the form h^{rs} × S = Hom(−, r) × Hom(−, s) × S, using |Hom(·, r) × Hom(·, s) × S| = Δ^r × Δ^s × S.
Every T has a canonical presentation as the coequaliser of ⊔ h^{r′s′} × T_{rs} ⇉ ⊔ h^{rs} × T_{rs} → T.
All three functors commute with colimits, so the homeomorphisms extend from representables to all T (Quillen §1 Lemma).
acceptance: The diagonal of the bisimplicial set T(f) in the proof of Theorem A is the nerve of S(f).
The realisation of the product bicategory A ⊗ B is BA × BB (Weibel IV Example 3.10.1).
Scope: this node does not supply the levelwise-equivalence theorem (H.2/levelwise-equivalence-theorem) nor the levelwise-fibration theorem (H.2/levelwise-fibration-realisation).

nodes.title: Proper simplicial spaces
nodes.statement: A simplicial space X is proper if for every n the latching map L_n X → X_n is a Hurewicz cofibration (has the homotopy extension property), where L_n X ⊆ X_n is the union of the images of the degeneracies s_i : X_{n−1} → X_n. Levelwise discrete simplicial spaces (simplicial sets) and the simplicial spaces p ↦ |T_{p,•}| obtained from bisimplicial sets are proper.
hypotheses: Spaces in compactly generated weak Hausdorff spaces for the realisation theorems that use properness (Nikolaus–Scholze Appendix C); the definition itself makes sense in TopCat.
proofSteps: Define the latching object as the coequaliser of the degeneracies (Nikolaus–Scholze Appendix C, before Proposition C.3).
For X = |T_{p,•}|, L_n X is the realisation of the simplicial subset of degenerate simplices, a subcomplex, and CW inclusions are h-cofibrations (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 4).
acceptance: The nerve of a topological category with degeneracies closed cofibrations is proper.

sources.locator: Appendix C, paragraph before Proposition C.3, p. 161
sources.excerpt: we call a simplicial space X• proper if all the maps Ln X → Xn are h-cofibrations

nodes.title: Realisation of simplicial spaces preserves finite limits
nodes.statement: In compactly generated weak Hausdorff spaces, the realisation |−| of simplicial spaces commutes with finite limits; in particular |X ×_Y Z| ≅ |X| ×_{|Y|} |Z| and |X × Z| ≅ |X| × |Z|.
hypotheses: All spaces compactly generated weak Hausdorff; limits formed there. In Mathlib's TopCat (not k-ified) only the product with a locally compact factor is covered.
For levelwise realisations of simplicial sets the compactly generated realisation agrees with the TopCat coend of H.2/simplicial-space-realisation (Nikolaus–Scholze p. 148).
proofSteps: Finite products: Schwede, Symmetric spectra, Proposition A.37(ii) (cited by Nikolaus–Scholze, not read here).

Pullbacks: the underlying-set functor of the realisation is the coend of underlying sets, which commutes with finite limits by Gabriel–Zisman III; the comparison is a continuous bijection between closed subspaces of a product (Nikolaus–Scholze Prop. C.1 proof).
acceptance: For bisimplicial sets this recovers |T × T′| ≅ |T| × |T′| in compactly generated spaces.

nodes.title: The gluing lemma for pushouts along h-cofibrations
nodes.statement: Given a map of spans (B ← A → C) → (B′ ← A′ → C′) in which A → B and A′ → B′ are Hurewicz cofibrations and the three components are weak homotopy equivalences, the induced map of pushouts B ∪_A C → B′ ∪_{A′} C′ is a weak homotopy equivalence.
hypotheses: A → B and A′ → B′ h-cofibrations; components weak homotopy equivalences; compactly generated weak Hausdorff spaces.
proofSteps: Boardman–Vogt, Proposition 4.8(b), cited by Nikolaus–Scholze Lemma C.2 (not read; recorded in the packet gap 'Gluing lemma proof').
acceptance: For an h-cofibration A → B and a weak homotopy equivalence g : C → C′ under A, B ∪_A C → B ∪_A C′ is a weak homotopy equivalence (span map (id, id, g)).

sources.locator: Appendix C, Lemma C.2 (Gluing Lemma), p. 161
sources.excerpt: Then also the induced map on pushouts B ∪A C → B ′ ∪A′ C ′ is a weak homotopy equivalence.
sources.match: Nikolaus–Scholze's Lemma C.2, citing Boardman–Vogt for the proof.

nodes.title: Pushout products of h-cofibrations (Strøm's product theorem)
nodes.statement: If S ⊆ X and T ⊆ Y are h-cofibrations (homotopy extension property for all targets) and T is closed in Y, then S × Y ∪ X × T ⊆ X × Y is an h-cofibration. In particular, for a proper simplicial space X, L_nX × Δⁿ ∪ X_n × ∂Δⁿ ⊆ X_n × Δⁿ is an h-cofibration.
hypotheses: T closed in Y (∂Δⁿ ⊆ Δⁿ in the application).
proofSteps: Represent the h-cofibrations by Strøm's data (u, H) for (X, S) and (v, K) for (Y, T) (a function vanishing on the subspace and a deformation into it where the function is below 1).
Combine them by w(x, y) = min(u x, v y) and the interpolated deformation to obtain such data for the product pair (Strøm, Note on cofibrations II, Math. Scand. 22 (1968); not supplied).
acceptance: For (Δᵖ, ∂Δᵖ) and (Δ^q, ∂Δ^q) it gives the boundary inclusion of Δᵖ × Δ^q.
For T = ∅ it reduces to S × Y ⊆ X × Y, an h-cofibration whenever S ⊆ X is.

sources.locator: Appendix C, proof of Proposition C.3, p. 161
sources.excerpt: If X• is proper the pushout product axiom implies that the upper morphism is an h-cofibration.
sources.match: Nikolaus–Scholze's use of the product theorem, cited without proof; Strøm's theorem itself is not among the supplied sources.

nodes.title: Levelwise weak equivalences of proper simplicial spaces realise to weak equivalences
nodes.statement: Let f : X → Y be a map of proper simplicial spaces such that every f_n : X_n → Y_n is a weak homotopy equivalence. Then |f| : |X| → |Y| is a weak homotopy equivalence. For bisimplicial sets: if each X_{p,•} → Y_{p,•} is a weak homotopy equivalence of realisations, then |X| → |Y| (equivalently |diag X| → |diag Y|) is a weak homotopy equivalence, and a homotopy equivalence since both are CW complexes.
hypotheses: X, Y proper (H.2/proper-simplicial-space); for bisimplicial sets properness is automatic.

Every X_n and Y_n compactly generated and Hausdorff (weak Hausdorff suffices); then the TopCat coend agrees with Nikolaus–Scholze's realisation in compactly generated weak Hausdorff spaces (p. 148), where the proof (gluing lemma, closed h-cofibrations) takes place. Realisations of simplicial sets satisfy this.
proofSteps: Filter |X| by skeleta; |Sk_n X| is the pushout of |Sk_{n−1} X| ← L_n X × |Δⁿ| ∪ X_n × |∂Δⁿ| → X_n × Δⁿ, whose top map is an h-cofibration when X is proper (pushout-product axiom) (Nikolaus–Scholze Prop. C.3 proof).
By induction on n and on the latching filtration, L_n X → L_n Y are weak equivalences, so |Sk_n X| → |Sk_n Y| are weak equivalences by the gluing lemma (H.2/gluing-lemma).
Pass to the colimit along h-cofibrations: homotopy groups commute with sequential colimits along closed cofibrations by compactness.

For bisimplicial sets apply the result to p ↦ |X_{p,•}| (proper by H.2/proper-simplicial-space) and use H.2/bisimplicial-realization-lemma; Whitehead (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 8) upgrades to a homotopy equivalence (Weibel IV Theorem 3.6.1(i)).
acceptance: Weibel IV Example 3.6.2: the canonical functor D\F → C is a homotopy equivalence, by projecting the bisimplicial set of pairs of strings onto NC.
Without properness the conclusion can fail; do not apply to arbitrary simplicial spaces.

sources.excerpt: Let f : X• → Y• be a map of proper simplicial spaces that is a levelwise weak homotopy equivalence. Then the realization |X• | → |Y• | is a weak homotopy equivalence as well.
sources.match: Nikolaus–Scholze's Proposition C.3 with the proof summarised in the steps.

sources.excerpt: If each simplicial map Xp,∗ → Yp,∗ is a homotopy equivalence, so is BX → BY .
sources.match: Weibel's bisimplicial-set form, cited from Waldhausen 1978 and Quillen.

nodes.title: Realisation of levelwise homotopy fibre sequences (Waldhausen, Bousfield–Friedlander)
nodes.statement: Let V → W → X be maps of bisimplicial sets, realised levelwise (n ↦ |V_n|, |W_n|, |X_n|, H.2/bisimplicial-realization-lemma), such that the composite V → X factors through a vertex x of X (each |V_n| → |X_n| is constant at the degenerate vertex x_n), each canonical map |V_n| → F(|W_n| → |X_n|, x_n), v ↦ (i v, const), is a weak homotopy equivalence, and every |X_n| is path-connected. Then the canonical map |V| → F(|W| → |X|, |x|), v ↦ (|i| v, const), is a weak homotopy equivalence, so |V| → |W| → |X| is a homotopy fibre sequence over the realised basepoint |x|, and Ω|X| → |V| → |W| → |X| is one with the canonical connecting map. For bases that are not levelwise connected see H.2/bisimplicial-fibration-pi-kan.
hypotheses: V, W, X bisimplicial sets, as in every consumer (GeneralAlgebraicKTheory:K.4 and H.5:S-delooping realise multisimplicial sets); their levelwise realisations are proper and CW, so no further cofibrancy hypothesis is needed.
Each |X_n| path-connected; the conclusion fails for arbitrary levelwise fibrations without it (acceptance example).
proofSteps: Replace V, W, X levelwise by Kan complexes (Ex^∞); by H.2/levelwise-equivalence-theorem in its bisimplicial form this changes the realisations by weak equivalences compatible with i, p and x.

Waldhausen 1978, Lemma 5.2, or Bousfield–Friedlander 1978, Theorem B.4 (connected bases make the π_*-Kan and π₀ conditions automatic): the realisation of the levelwise quasi-fibrations is a quasi-fibration (H.2/quasi-fibration and the Dold–Lashof criteria). These proofs are not read here (packet gap 'Levelwise fibration lemma proof').
acceptance: Weibel V Proposition 1.7: for an exact functor f : B → C, Ω|wS.(S.B)| → |wS.C| → |wS.(S.f)| → |wS.(S.B)| is a homotopy fibration, by applying the lemma to n ↦ (|wS.C| → |wS.(S_n f)| → |wS.(S_n B)|), which are split fibrations of connected spaces (S_n f ≃ E(C, S_n f, S_n B) by Weibel IV 8.5.3; Weibel's proof of V.1.7 prints the roles of B and C exchanged, packet source issue StableHomotopyKTheory/E4).

Connectivity is needed: for X = Δ[1]/∂Δ[1] viewed as a levelwise discrete simplicial space, each ∗ → ∗ → X_n is a homotopy fibre sequence (X_n is discrete), but after realisation ∗ → ∗ → S¹ is not, the homotopy fibre of ∗ → S¹ being ΩS¹ ≃ ℤ; here X_n is disconnected for n ≥ 1.

sources.excerpt: But if X. → Y. → Z. is any sequence of simplicial spaces, and each Xn → Yn → Zn is a fibration with Zn connected, then Ω|Z.| → |X.| → |Y.| → |Z.| is a homotopy fibration sequence; see [Wa78, 5.2].
sources.match: Weibel's statement of the lemma inside the proof of V.1.7, citing Waldhausen 1978, Lemma 5.2.

nodes.title: Realisation of levelwise fibre sequences under the π_*-Kan condition (Bousfield–Friedlander)
nodes.statement: Let V → W → X be maps of bisimplicial sets such that V → X factors through a vertex x of X (each |V_m| → |X_m| is constant at x_m) and each canonical map |V_m| → F(|W_m| → |X_m|, x_m) is a weak homotopy equivalence. Suppose W and X satisfy the π_*-Kan condition of Bousfield–Friedlander (Definition B.3.1: for every t ≥ 1 the simplicial sets of t-th vertical homotopy groups over the vertical vertices form Kan fibrations, after levelwise Kan replacement) and that π₀^v W → π₀^v X, m ↦ (π₀|W_m| → π₀|X_m|), is a Kan fibration. Then the canonical map |V| → F(|W| → |X|, |x|), v ↦ (|i| v, const), is a weak homotopy equivalence. If every |W_m| and |X_m| is path-connected, all three conditions hold.
hypotheses: Bisimplicial sets, realised as in H.2/bisimplicial-realization-lemma.

The π_*-Kan condition is phrased with homotopy groups of Kan complexes imported from Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 8; its exact form is Bousfield–Friedlander's Definition B.3.1, which was not read and must be pinned when the gap 'Levelwise fibration lemma proof' is closed.
proofSteps: Replace V, W, X levelwise by Kan complexes; this changes the realisations by weak equivalences compatible with the maps (H.2/levelwise-equivalence-theorem, bisimplicial form).
Bousfield–Friedlander 1978, Theorem B.4 (not read; gap 'Levelwise fibration lemma proof'; Goerss–Jardine IV.4 is the textbook form named there).
acceptance: Segal's simplicial path fibration of a special grouplike Γ-space (H.4/segal-delooping-theorem), whose base levels X(m) ≃ X(1)^m are not connected, satisfies the hypotheses; the connected form H.2/levelwise-fibration-realisation does not apply there.

In the counterexample of H.2/levelwise-fibration-realisation (∗ → ∗ → Δ[1]/∂Δ[1]) the map π₀^v W = ∗ → π₀^v X = Δ[1]/∂Δ[1] is not a Kan fibration (the nondegenerate 1-simplex has no lift), as the failure of the conclusion requires.

sources.excerpt: But if X. → Y. → Z. is any sequence of simplicial spaces, and each Xn → Yn → Zn is a fibration with Zn connected
sources.match: The connected special case as Weibel quotes it from Waldhausen 1978, 5.2; the π_*-Kan form is Bousfield–Friedlander's Theorem B.4, which is not among the supplied sources.

nodes.title: Bousfield–Kan homotopy colimit of a diagram of spaces
nodes.statement: For a small category I and X : I ⥤ TopCat, hocolim_I X is the realisation of the simplicial space n ↦ ⊔_{i₀ → ⋯ → i_n} X(i₀) (sum over n-simplices of NI), with d₀ using X(i₀ → i₁) and the other faces and degeneracies acting on the string. It maps to BI (collapse each X(i₀) to a point); for X constant at a point, hocolim_I X = BI; for X : I ⥤ Type (discrete spaces), hocolim_I X = B(∫_I X). Convention: Nikolaus–Scholze print X(i_n) in Definition C.4, which is the formula for contravariant X; with covariant X and strings i₀ → ⋯ → i_n the coefficient is X(i₀).
hypotheses: I small; X a covariant functor to TopCat.
proofSteps: Define the simplicial space with the face maps above; it is proper because its latching object is the inclusion of a union of summands (Nikolaus–Scholze, after Definition C.4).
Homotopy invariance (Proposition C.5): a levelwise weak equivalence X → X′ induces a weak equivalence of hocolims, by H.2/levelwise-equivalence-theorem.
acceptance: hocolim of the constant point diagram is BI.
For I the walking span, hocolim is the double mapping cylinder.

sources.locator: Appendix C, Definition C.4 and Proposition C.5, p. 162
sources.excerpt: The (Bousfield-Kan) homotopy colimit of X is defined as the geo-metric realization
sources.match: Nikolaus–Scholze's definition; the printed X(i_n) is the known misprint PAPER-NIKOLAUS-SCHOLZE-18/E18, corrected to X(i₀) for covariant X.
