nodes.title: Realisation of a proper simplicial space is its homotopy colimit
nodes.statement: Let X be a proper simplicial space (H.2/proper-simplicial-space) in compactly generated weak Hausdorff spaces. Then the natural comparison map hocolim_{Δ^op} X → |X| from the Bousfield–Kan homotopy colimit (H.2/bousfield-kan-homotopy-colimit), induced by the last-vertex maps B(Δ↓[n]) → Δⁿ, is a weak homotopy equivalence. The ∞-categorical form of Nikolaus–Scholze Lemma B.7 (realisation of proper simplicial spaces models the ∞-colimit) follows from this together with Nikolaus–Scholze Prop. C.5 and is stated by its consumer RefinedTraceMethods:RT.2.
hypotheses: X proper; all spaces compactly generated weak Hausdorff (so h-cofibrations are closed, Nikolaus–Scholze footnote 44).
Without properness the statement holds for the fat realisation over Δ_inj instead (Nikolaus–Scholze Remark B.8); it is not claimed for |−|.
proofSteps: Choose a Reedy cofibrant replacement X̃ → X, a levelwise weak homotopy equivalence with X̃ proper (packet gap 'Reedy model structure on simplicial spaces').
For Reedy cofibrant X̃ the Bousfield–Kan comparison map hocolim_{Δ^op} X̃ → |X̃| is a weak homotopy equivalence (Hirschhorn Theorem 18.7.4; same gap).

In the naturality square, |X̃| → |X| is a weak equivalence by H.2/levelwise-equivalence-theorem and hocolim X̃ → hocolim X by H.2/bousfield-kan-homotopy-colimit (Nikolaus–Scholze Prop. C.5); conclude by two-out-of-three (H.2/weak-homotopy-equivalence).
acceptance: For a simplicial set K viewed as a levelwise discrete simplicial space (proper by H.2/proper-simplicial-space), hocolim_{Δ^op} K = B(Δ↓K)^op ≃ |K| (H.2/bousfield-kan-homotopy-colimit, discrete case): the simplex category of K has the homotopy type of K.

For the constant simplicial space at Y (proper: its latching inclusions are identities), |X| = Y and hocolim_{Δ^op} X = Y × B(Δ^op) ≃ Y, since Δ has the terminal object [0] and so BΔ is contractible (H.1/contractible-of-initial-or-terminal).

nodes.title: Quillen's quasi-fibration lemma for diagrams of spaces over a nerve
nodes.statement: Let I be a small category and i ↦ X_i a functor to topological spaces, and let g : X_I → BI be the realisation of the map from p ↦ ⊔_{i₀→⋯→i_p} X_{i₀} to the nerve of I (that is, hocolim_I X → BI). If every induced map X_i → X_{i′} is a homotopy equivalence then g is a quasi-fibration: for every b ∈ BI the map g⁻¹(b) → F(g, b) is a weak homotopy equivalence. In particular, for every object i, g⁻¹([i]) = X_i and the square X_i → X_I over {[i]} → BI is homotopy-cartesian.
hypotheses: Every transition map X_i → X_{i′} (for arrows i → i′ of I) is a homotopy equivalence.
The proof uses the Dold–Lashof criteria including disconnected fibres (H.2/dold-lashof-criteria).
proofSteps: By the Dold–Lashof criterion (b) (H.2/dold-lashof-exhaustion; compact subsets of BI lie in finite skeleta) it suffices to show g restricted to each skeleton F_p of BI is a quasi-fibration.
Let U be F_p minus the barycentres of the p-cells and V = F_p − F_{p−1}; by criterion (a) it suffices to treat U, V and U ∩ V; over each open p-cell g is a product, which handles V and U ∩ V.
For U apply criterion (c) (H.2/dold-lashof-deformation) using induction on p and the radial fibre-preserving deformation of Δ^p minus its barycentre onto ∂Δ^p.

If the deformation moves x in the cell of i₀ → ⋯ → i_p to the face with vertices j₀ < ⋯ < j_q, then g⁻¹(x) = X_{i₀}, g⁻¹(x′) = X_{k₀} with k₀ = i_{j₀}, and the induced map is the transition map of i₀ → k₀, a homotopy equivalence by hypothesis (Quillen §1 Lemma proof).
acceptance: Applied to Y ↦ B(Y\f) under the hypothesis of Theorem B, yields that BS(f) → BC′^op is a quasi-fibration.

Applied to the map realising q ↦ (⊔ B(C′/fX₀)^op → NC_q), whose fibres have final objects and so are contractible, it promotes these levelwise homotopy equivalences to the homotopy equivalence Bp₁ in the proof of Theorem A (Quillen's alternative to Tornehave A.3).

nodes.title: Thomason's theorem: the Grothendieck construction models the homotopy colimit
nodes.statement: For a small category D and a functor F : D ⥤ Cat, there is a canonical weak homotopy equivalence hocolim_D (B ∘ F) → B(∫_D F), natural in F; equivalently the diagonal of the bisimplicial set δN(D, F) with (n, m)-simplices pairs (d₀ → ⋯ → d_n, a string of length m in F(d₀)) maps by a weak equivalence to the nerve of the Grothendieck construction. For a functor T : C ⥤ D and F_T(d) = T/d, the projection ∫_D F_T → C has a left adjoint, so BC ≃ B(∫_D F_T) ≃ hocolim_d B(T/d).
hypotheses: D small; F takes values in small categories; the Grothendieck construction is Mathlib's CategoryTheory.Grothendieck.
proofSteps: Thomason 1979, Theorem 1.2 (cited by Kahn, Theorem 1.4.3; proof not read here, recorded in the packet gap 'Thomason homotopy colimit theorem proof'): the comparison map sends a pair of strings to the composite string in ∫_D F.

For T : C ⥤ D, ∫_D (T/−) is the comma category T/D; the source functor s : C → T/D, c ↦ (c, id) is left adjoint to the projection p₁ (Kahn Lemma 1.4.5), hence a homotopy equivalence (H.1/adjunction-homotopy-equivalence).
acceptance: For F constant at a category E, B(D × E) ≃ BD × BE.
For F : D ⥤ Type (discrete categories) it reduces to hocolim_D F = B(∫_D F) of H.2/bousfield-kan-homotopy-colimit.

sources.excerpt: There is a canonical weak equivalence δN(D, F) → N(D ∫ F)

nodes.title: The homology spectral sequence of a functor
nodes.statement: For a functor T : C ⥤ D between small categories and an abelian group A there is a first-quadrant spectral sequence E²_{p,q} = H_p(D; d ↦ H_q(T/d; A)) ⇒ H_{p+q}(C; A), natural in T, with H_p(D; −) the homology of D with coefficients in a functor (H.1/category-homology). If T is cofibred, the coefficient functor may be replaced by d ↦ H_q(T⁻¹(d); A), recovering Weibel IV Exercise 3.7.
hypotheses: C, D small; A an abelian group (or a module over a ring).
proofSteps: Form the double complex with (p, q)-generators the pairs (c₀ → ⋯ → c_q, T(c_q) → d₀ → ⋯ → d_p) (tensor A). For a fixed C-string the D-direction is the nerve of T(c_q)\D, which has an initial object (H.1/contractible-of-initial-or-terminal), so the column filtration gives H_*(C; A).

For a fixed D-string d₀ → ⋯ → d_p the C-direction is the nerve of T/d₀, functorial in d₀ along d₀ → d₁; so the row filtration has E¹_{p,q} = ⊕ H_q(T/d₀; A) and E² = H_p(D; d ↦ H_q(T/d; A)) in the convention of H.1/category-homology (coefficient at the first vertex). For cofibred T, T⁻¹(d) → T/d has a left adjoint, giving the T⁻¹(d) form.

Construct the spectral sequence from the double complex with Mathlib's spectral objects (CategoryTheory.Abelian.SpectralObject and its E₂ homological spectral sequence), first-quadrant convergence being automatic.
acceptance: For T = id the E² page is concentrated in q = 0 and the spectral sequence collapses.
For the projection ρ : S⁻¹X → ⟨S, S⟩ (cofibred with fibre X) it gives the spectral sequence of Weibel IV Theorem 4.8.

sources.excerpt: Then show that the row filtration yields a spectral sequence converging to H∗ (C; Z) with Epq = Hp (D; Hq F −1 )
sources.match: Weibel's exercise for a cofibred functor; its printed double complex has rows d₀\F and is corrected in the proof steps (source issue on Ex. 3.7).

sources.excerpt: There is a spectral sequence Ep,q = Hp (D, Hq (FT , A)) ⇒ Hp+q (C, A)

nodes.title: Quillen's Theorem A
nodes.statement: Let f : C ⥤ C′ be a functor between small categories. If the comma category Y\f of pairs (X, v : Y → fX) is contractible for every object Y of C′, then Bf is a homotopy equivalence. Dually, it suffices that every f/Y be contractible.
hypotheses: C, C′ small.
proofSteps: Form S(f), the category of triples (X, Y, v : Y → fX), with functors p₁ : S(f) → C and p₂ : S(f) → C′^op.
Let T(f) be the bisimplicial set of pairs (Y_p → ⋯ → Y₀ → fX₀, X₀ → ⋯ → X_q); its diagonal is NS(f) (H.2/bisimplicial-realization-lemma), and forgetting the first component realises to Bp₁.

Realising in p gives, in each q, ⊔_{X₀→⋯→X_q} B(C′/fX₀)^op → NC_q, a homotopy equivalence since C′/fX₀ has a final object; by H.2/levelwise-equivalence-theorem (or the quasi-fibration lemma) Bp₁ is a homotopy equivalence.
Realising T(f) → N(C′^op) in q gives fibres B(Y₀\f), contractible by hypothesis, so p₂ is a homotopy equivalence.

Compare with f = id_{C′} through S(f) → S(id_{C′}), (X, Y, v) ↦ (fX, Y, v), compatible with p₁ and p₂; since Y\id_{C′} has an initial object the same argument applies, and two-out-of-three gives Bf a homotopy equivalence.
The dual statement follows by applying the theorem to f^op and H.1/classifying-space-op-homeomorph.
acceptance: A simplicial map of simplicial complexes whose inverse image of every closed simplex is contractible is a homotopy equivalence (Quillen's example).
The inclusion of monoids ℕ → ℤ gives Bℕ ≃ Bℤ ≃ S¹ (Weibel IV Example 3.7.2).
Source and target functors from the Segal subdivision are homotopy equivalences (Weibel IV Exercise 3.9).

nodes.title: Quillen's prefibred functors are SGA 1 prefibered functors
nodes.statement: For a functor f : C ⥤ C′, the inclusion of the fibre f⁻¹(Y) into the comma category Y\f has a right adjoint for every Y (Quillen's and Weibel's 'prefibred') iff f is prefibered in the sense of SGA 1 VI.6.1 (Mathlib's CategoryTheory.Functor.IsPreFibered: every u : Y → f(X) has a cartesian lift). In that case B(f⁻¹(Y)) ≃ B(Y\f), and base change u* : f⁻¹(Y′) → f⁻¹(Y) is defined up to natural isomorphism as f⁻¹(Y′) → Y\f → f⁻¹(Y). Dually for precofibred and F/Y.
hypotheses: f a functor between small categories.
proofSteps: A right adjoint to f⁻¹(Y) → Y\f assigns to (X, u : Y → fX) an object u*X of f⁻¹(Y) with a map u*X → X over u, terminal among maps from objects of the fibre over u: this is a cartesian lift of u in the sense of SGA 1 (and Mathlib's IsCartesian).
An adjoint gives a homotopy equivalence (H.1/adjunction-homotopy-equivalence; Weibel IV 3.7.3).
acceptance: The projection ∫_C F → C of a Grothendieck construction of F : C^op ⥤ Cat is prefibred, with base change F(u); dually, for Mathlib's CategoryTheory.Grothendieck F (F : C ⥤ Cat) the projection is precofibred with cobase change F(u).

sources.locator: Fibered and Cofibered functors 3.7.3, p. IV.31
sources.excerpt: We say that a functor F : C → D is pre-fibered if for every d in D the inclusion F −1 (d) ֒→ d\F has a right adjoint.
sources.match: Weibel's definition (following SGA 1), and the consequence BF⁻¹(d) ≃ B(d\F); the comparison with cartesian lifts is packet-authored.

nodes.title: Theorem A for prefibred and precofibred functors
nodes.statement: If f : C ⥤ C′ is prefibred or precofibred and every fibre f⁻¹(Y) is contractible, then Bf is a homotopy equivalence.
hypotheses: f prefibred (H.2/prefibred-iff-fibre-adjoint) or precofibred; fibres contractible.
proofSteps: The adjoint gives B(f⁻¹(Y)) ≃ B(Y\f) (respectively B(f/Y)), so the comma categories are contractible; apply H.2/quillen-theorem-a or its dual (Quillen §1 Corollary to Theorem A; Weibel IV Corollary 3.7.4).
acceptance: The projection of a Grothendieck construction with contractible fibres is a homotopy equivalence.

nodes.title: Quillen's Theorem B
nodes.statement: Let f : C ⥤ C′ be a functor such that for every arrow u : Y → Y′ of C′ the induced functor u* : Y′\f → Y\f is a homotopy equivalence. Then for every object Y of C′ the square with Y\f → C over Y\C′ → C′ is homotopy-cartesian, so the canonical map B(Y\f) → F(Bf, [Y]) of H.2/comma-category-to-homotopy-fibre is a weak homotopy equivalence, and for X ∈ f⁻¹(Y) there is an exact sequence ⋯ → π_{i+1}(BC′, [Y]) → π_i(B(Y\f), (X, id_Y)) → π_i(BC, [X]) → π_i(BC′, [Y]) → ⋯ ending in pointed sets. Dually with f/Y.
hypotheses: Every transition functor Y′\f → Y\f is a homotopy equivalence; contractibility of comma categories alone (Theorem A) does not produce a fibration sequence.
Weak homotopy equivalence in the homotopy-cartesian definition (H.2/homotopy-pullback); spaces involved are CW complexes, so these are homotopy equivalences.
proofSteps: As in Theorem A, p₁ : S(f) → C is a homotopy equivalence.

Bp₂ : BS(f) → BC′^op is the realisation of T(f) → N(C′^op); apply the quasi-fibration lemma to Y ↦ B(Y\f), whose transition maps are homotopy equivalences by hypothesis, so Bp₂ is a quasi-fibration and the square Y\f → S(f) over pt → C′^op is homotopy-cartesian.

Form the diagram with squares (1) Y\f → S(f) over Y\C′ → S(id_{C′}), (2) S(f) → C over S(id_{C′}) → C′, and (3) Y\C′ → S(id_{C′}) over pt → C′^op; the horizontal comparison maps marked are homotopy equivalences.

(1)+(3) is homotopy-cartesian by the previous step and (3) is homotopy-cartesian, so (1) is (H.2/homotopy-cartesian-pasting, transposed form for vertical pasting); composing with (2), whose horizontal maps are homotopy equivalences, gives the theorem (Quillen, proof of Theorem B).
The exact sequence is H.2/long-exact-sequence for Bf with the fibre identified.

B(Y\C′) is contractible (initial object (Y, id_Y), H.1/contractible-of-initial-or-terminal); by H.2/homotopy-cartesian-contractible-base with the contraction given by the initial object, whose composite with Bj′ is the homotopy of the transformation const_Y ⇒ j′ and pulls back to const_Y ⇒ f ∘ j, the homotopy-cartesian square makes commaToHomotopyFiber a weak homotopy equivalence.
acceptance: The target functor t : EA → QA is fibred, but Theorem B does not apply to it unless A ≅ 0 (Weibel IV Exercise 7.4); S⁻¹EA → QA does satisfy it for split exact A (Weibel IV Theorem 7.8).
The long exact sequence keeps the basepoint (X, id_Y) and the pointed-set end terms.
Additivity and localisation consumers must verify the transition hypothesis for their specific functors.

nodes.title: Theorem B for prefibred functors
nodes.statement: If f is prefibred and every base change u* : f⁻¹(Y′) → f⁻¹(Y) is a homotopy equivalence (or f precofibred with every cobase change a homotopy equivalence), then for every Y the sequence f⁻¹(Y) → C → C′ realises to a homotopy fibre sequence, with the long exact sequence ⋯ → π_{i+1}(BC′) → π_i(B f⁻¹(Y)) → π_i(BC) → π_i(BC′) → ⋯.
hypotheses: f prefibred with base changes homotopy equivalences, or precofibred with cobase changes homotopy equivalences.
proofSteps: The adjoint identifications B(f⁻¹(Y)) ≃ B(Y\f) (H.2/prefibred-iff-fibre-adjoint) are compatible with u* and the base changes, so the transition functors of comma categories are homotopy equivalences; apply H.2/quillen-theorem-b, and identify the fibre map with commaToHomotopyFiber on the strict fibre (api commaToHomotopyFiber_fiberToComma of H.2/comma-category-to-homotopy-fibre) (Weibel IV Corollary 3.8.1, Exercise 3.6).
acceptance: For a surjective group homomorphism G → Q with kernel N the cobase changes are conjugations, giving BN → BG → BQ (H.2/group-extension-fibration).

nodes.title: Classifying spaces of a group extension form a fibre sequence
nodes.statement: For a short exact sequence of groups 1 → N → G → Q → 1, the sequence BN → BG → BQ is a homotopy fibre sequence; in particular π₁ gives back 1 → N → G → Q → 1 and π_n vanish for n ≥ 2. For a central extension 1 → A → S → P → 1 this is the input to the plus-construction fibration BA → BS⁺ → BP⁺ (H.3/plus-uce-fibration).
hypotheses: N normal in G with quotient Q.
proofSteps: The functor SingleObj G ⥤ SingleObj Q is precofibred with fibre SingleObj N: an object of f/∗ is an element q ∈ Q, and the inclusion of the fibre has a left adjoint choosing lifts; cobase change along q ∈ Q is conjugation by a lift of q, an isomorphism of SingleObj N up to natural isomorphism.
Apply H.2/quillen-theorem-b-prefibred (Weibel IV Exercise 3.6(c)).
acceptance: For G = N × Q the fibre sequence splits.
For ℤ → ℤ → ℤ/n (multiplication by n): Bℤ ≃ S¹ → S¹ → B(ℤ/n).

nodes.title: Acyclic spaces
nodes.statement: A topological space F is acyclic if its reduced integral singular homology vanishes: H̃_n(F; ℤ) = 0 for all n (equivalently F is nonempty, path-connected and H_n(F; ℤ) = 0 for n ≥ 1). Group homology with nontrivial local coefficients, not trivial-coefficient cohomology, is what acyclic maps test (H.3/acyclic-map-homology-criterion).
hypotheses: F any topological space; singular homology as in Mathlib (AlgebraicTopology.singularHomologyFunctor).
proofSteps: Define IsAcyclicSpace F by vanishing of reduced integral singular homology (Weibel IV Definition 1.3).
Path-connectedness follows from H₀(F; ℤ) = ℤ (Mathlib's singularHomology₀ computation).
acceptance: A contractible space is acyclic.
The Volodin space X(R) ⊂ BGL(R) is acyclic with π₁ image E(R) (Weibel IV Example 1.3.2, cited from Suslin).
BG for a perfect group with H₂(G) = 0 is not acyclic in general (it has H₃).

sources.excerpt: We call a topological space F acyclic if it has the homology of a point
sources.match: Weibel's definition, taken from Hausmann–Husemoller and Berrick.

nodes.title: Hurewicz in degree one
nodes.statement: For a path-connected space X and x ∈ X, regarding loops as singular 1-cycles gives a homomorphism h : π₁(X, x) → H₁(X; ℤ) which is surjective with kernel the commutator subgroup; hence π₁(X, x)^{ab} ≅ H₁(X; ℤ), naturally in based maps.
hypotheses: X path-connected; singular homology with integer coefficients (Mathlib singularHomologyFunctor).
proofSteps: Define h on paths and check it respects homotopy rel endpoints (a homotopy gives a singular 2-chain whose boundary is the difference) and concatenation (the 2-simplex filling a concatenation).
Surjectivity and kernel: Hatcher's proof of Theorem 2A.1 (choose paths from x to every point to turn a 1-cycle into a product of loops; a 1-cycle that bounds gives a product of commutators).
acceptance: For X = S¹ this is π₁ ≅ ℤ ≅ H₁.
AT stage 8 item 3 covers only n ≥ 2; this node supplies the degree-one case used by H.3/acyclic-space-perfect-fundamental-group.

sources.excerpt: If X is path-connected, then h is surjective and has kernel the commutator subgroup of π1 (X) , so h induces an isomorphism from the abelian- ization of π1 (X) onto H1 (X) .
sources.match: Statement and proof followed.

nodes.title: An acyclic space has perfect fundamental group with vanishing H₂
nodes.statement: If F is acyclic then F is path-connected, G = π₁(F) is perfect, and H₂(G; ℤ) = 0.
hypotheses: F acyclic and of CW homotopy type (so that F → BG classifying the universal cover exists).
proofSteps: H₀(F) = ℤ gives connectedness; G/[G, G] ≅ H₁(F; ℤ) = 0 (H.3/hurewicz-degree-one) gives perfectness.

Attach cells of dimension ≥ 3 to F to kill π_{≥2} (Hatcher Example 4.16 with n = 1); the result F₁ is a K(G, 1), hence homotopy equivalent to BG (H.3/eilenberg-maclane-space, uniqueness for n = 1), and the homotopy fibre of F → F₁ is the universal cover F̃ (H.2/long-exact-sequence), with H₁(F̃; ℤ) = 0 (H.3/hurewicz-degree-one).

The Serre spectral sequence E²_{pq} = H_p(BG; H_q(F̃; ℤ)) ⇒ H_{p+q}(F; ℤ) (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 5, infinite-CW base) has E²_{p,1} = 0, so H₂(F) maps onto E^∞_{2,0} = E²_{2,0} = H₂(BG; ℤ) ≅ H₂(G; ℤ) (H.1/bar-complex-comparison); hence H₂(G; ℤ) = 0 (Weibel IV Lemma 1.3.1).
acceptance: For the Poincaré sphere minus a point, π₁ is the binary icosahedral group, perfect with H₂ = 0.

sources.excerpt: Let F be an acyclic space. Then F is connected, its fundamental group G = π1 (F ) is a perfect group, and H2 (G; Z) = 0 as well.
sources.match: Weibel's lemma and its proof via the Serre spectral sequence of F̃ → F → BG.

nodes.title: Acyclic maps
nodes.statement: A map f : X → Y of based path-connected spaces of CW homotopy type is acyclic if its homotopy fibre F(f, y₀) is acyclic. Then π₁(X) → π₁(Y) is surjective and its kernel is a perfect normal subgroup (H.3/acyclic-map-fundamental-group).
hypotheses: X, Y based path-connected of CW homotopy type; homotopy fibre over the basepoint (any basepoint gives a homotopy-equivalent fibre, H.2/homotopy-fibre-transport).
proofSteps: Define IsAcyclicMap f := IsAcyclicSpace (homotopyFiber f y₀) (Weibel IV Definition 1.4).
Independence of the basepoint: transport of homotopy fibres along paths (H.2/homotopy-fibre-transport).
acceptance: X → point is acyclic iff X is acyclic (Weibel IV Example 1.4.2).
A homotopy equivalence is acyclic.

nodes.title: Acyclic maps are surjective on π₁ with perfect kernel
nodes.statement: If f : X → Y is acyclic then π₁(X) → π₁(Y) is surjective and its kernel P is a perfect normal subgroup of π₁(X), namely the image of the perfect group π₁(F(f)).
hypotheses: f acyclic.
proofSteps: The homotopy fibre is path-connected and π₁F(f) is perfect (H.3/acyclic-space-perfect-fundamental-group).

Exactness of π₁F(f) → π₁X → π₁Y → π₀F(f) = * (H.2/long-exact-sequence) gives surjectivity, and the kernel is the image of a perfect group, hence perfect (Weibel IV Definition 1.4 and the following remark).
acceptance: For BGL(R) → BGL(R)⁺ the kernel is E(R).

nodes.title: Homology with local coefficients through a regular cover
nodes.statement: Let X be a path-connected space with a universal cover (for instance a connected CW complex), π = π₁(X, x), N ⊆ π a normal subgroup and X_N → X the regular cover with deck group π/N. For a ℤ[π/N]-module M, viewed as a local coefficient system on X (Tau Ceti AT stage 2), the twisted singular chains satisfy C_*(X; M) ≅ C_*(X_N) ⊗_{ℤ[π/N]} M naturally, and C_n(X_N) is a free ℤ[π/N]-module. In particular H_*(X; ℤ[π/N]) ≅ H_*(X_N; ℤ). The same holds for a pair (X, A) and the preimage of A.
hypotheses: X path-connected, locally path-connected and semilocally simply connected; M a left ℤ[π/N]-module.
proofSteps: Singular simplices of X_N over a simplex σ of X form a free π/N-orbit (unique lifting of simplices, which are simply connected), so C_n(X_N) is free on chosen lifts.
Identify both sides with the quotient of C_n(X_N) ⊗ M by (γσ̃) ⊗ m ∼ σ̃ ⊗ γ⁻¹m (Hatcher Prop. 3H.4 and Example 3H.2); compatibility with boundaries and naturality are routine.
acceptance: N = π, M = ℤ: the constant-coefficient case (Hatcher Example 3H.1).
M = ℤ[π]: H_*(X; ℤ[π]) ≅ H_*(X̃) (Hatcher Example 3H.2), the identification used in Weibel IV Lemma 1.6.

sources.excerpt: If X is a path-connected space having a universal covering space, then the groups Hn (X; E) are naturally isomorphic to the homology groups Hn (X; G) with local coefficients in the Z[π ] module G associated to E , where π = π1 (X) .
sources.match: Twisted (bundle) chains agree with C(X̃) ⊗_π G; Example 3H.2 (p. 329) gives the cover form.

nodes.title: Comparison of Serre spectral sequences: base and total space determine the fibre
nodes.statement: Let (F → E → B) → (F′ → E′ → B′) be a map of Serre fibrations over path-connected CW bases such that π₁(B) acts trivially on H_*(F; ℤ) and π₁(B′) on H_*(F′; ℤ). If B → B′ and E → E′ induce isomorphisms on H_*(−; ℤ), so does F → F′. Special case used by H.3/acyclic-map-homology-criterion: if B is simply connected and E → B is an integral homology isomorphism, the fibre is acyclic.
hypotheses: Trivial monodromy on the integral homology of both fibres; coefficients ℤ (a PID).
proofSteps: Special case (B simply connected, compare with ∗ → B → B): if H̃_q(F) = 0 for q < k, then E²_{p,q} = 0 for 0 < q < k, the edge map H_p(E) → E^∞_{p,0} ⊆ H_p(B) is the induced map (naturality, AT stage 5), which is onto, so no differential leaves the bottom row; nothing can hit E_{0,k} = H_k(F); and F_{k−1}H_k(E) ≅ E^∞_{0,k} = H_k(F) is the kernel of an isomorphism, so H_k(F) = 0.

General case: Zeeman's comparison theorem for first-quadrant spectral sequences over a PID applied to the two Serre spectral sequences and their map (AT stage 5); Hatcher SSAT states the result but omits this case, so it is recorded as a gap (MacLane, Homology, not read).
acceptance: E = B × F′ with F′ acyclic: the projection is a homology isomorphism.
Hatcher Example 4.35 shows the trivial-action hypothesis cannot be dropped: S¹ ⊂ X is a homology isomorphism over the base S¹ = B(ℤ) with non-acyclic fibre.

sources.excerpt: Then if two of the three maps F →F 0 , B →B 0 , and X →X 0 induce isomorphisms on H∗ (−; R) with R a principal ideal domain, so does the third.
sources.match: Statement; SSAT proves the other two cases and omits the case needed here.

nodes.title: Acyclic maps are local-coefficient homology isomorphisms
nodes.statement: A map f : X → Y of connected CW complexes is acyclic if and only if H_*(X; M) → H_*(Y; M) is an isomorphism for every π₁(Y)-module M (pulled back to X).
hypotheses: X, Y connected CW complexes; M ranges over all π₁(Y)-modules, including ℤ[π₁Y].

Uses the Serre spectral sequence with local coefficients in the base (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 5 constructs it with the monodromy system H_q(F; R) for a constant ring R); the twisted-coefficient form needed here is derived through the universal cover in both directions, recorded as the packet gap 'Serre spectral sequence with twisted total-space coefficients'. The infinite-CW-base form of the AT stage 5 spectral sequence is used (first quadrant, exhaustive skeletal filtration).
proofSteps: If f is acyclic, π₁F(f) → π₁Y is trivial, so π₁F(f) acts trivially on M and H_q(F(f); M) = 0 for q ≠ 0 by universal coefficients; the Serre spectral sequence H_p(Y; H_q(F(f); M)) ⇒ H_{p+q}(X; M) collapses. (With constant total-space coefficients only, this direction is run through the universal cover as in step 3.)

Conversely, if π₁Y = 0 and f is an integral homology isomorphism, the comparison of the Serre spectral sequences of F(f) → X → Y and ∗ → Y → Y (H.3/serre-comparison-fibre, simply connected special case) gives H̃_*(F(f); ℤ) = 0.

In general pass to the universal cover Ỹ and X̃ = X ×_Y Ỹ: H_*(Ỹ; ℤ) ≅ H_*(Y; ℤ[π₁Y]) and H_*(X̃; ℤ) ≅ H_*(X; ℤ[π₁Y]) (H.3/twisted-homology-via-cover), so X̃ → Ỹ is an integral homology isomorphism with simply connected target, and F(f̃) ≃ F(f) because the pullback square of the covering map is homotopy-cartesian (H.2/homotopy-pullback; Weibel IV Lemma 1.6 proof). The forward direction for arbitrary M follows the same way: C_*(X̃) → C_*(Ỹ) is a quasi-isomorphism of bounded-below free ℤ[π₁Y]-complexes, hence a chain homotopy equivalence, and C_*(−; M) = C_*(−̃) ⊗_{ℤ[π₁Y]} M.
acceptance: An integral homology isomorphism with non-perfect kernel on π₁ is not acyclic; test with a map inducing an isomorphism on integral homology only.
The comparison must be proved for ℤ[π₁Y] coefficients, not only for trivial modules.

sources.excerpt: A map f : X → Y is acyclic if and only if H∗ (X, M ) ∼ = H∗ (Y, M ) for every π1 (Y )-module M .

nodes.title: Plus constructions as acyclic maps
nodes.statement: For a based connected CW complex X and a perfect normal subgroup P ⊆ π₁(X), a map f : X → Y is a plus construction relative to P if f is acyclic and P is the kernel of π₁(X) → π₁(Y). The notation X⁺ means the plus construction relative to the perfect radical (largest perfect subgroup) of π₁(X).
hypotheses: X based connected CW complex; P perfect and normal in π₁(X).
proofSteps: Define IsPlusConstruction f P := IsAcyclicMap f ∧ ker (π₁ f) = P (Weibel IV Definition 1.4.1).
The perfect radical exists: the subgroup generated by all perfect subgroups is perfect and normal (Weibel IV Exercise 1.5).
acceptance: If X is acyclic, X → point is a plus construction relative to π₁(X) (Weibel IV Example 1.4.2).
Relative to P = 1, plus constructions are homotopy equivalences (H.3/acyclic-pi1-iso-weak-equivalence; Weibel IV Exercise 1.2(b)).

nodes.title: Acyclic maps that are isomorphisms on π₁
nodes.statement: Let f : X → Y be an acyclic map of path-connected spaces inducing an isomorphism π₁(X, x) → π₁(Y, f x). Then f is a weak homotopy equivalence, and a homotopy equivalence if X and Y are CW complexes. Conversely a weak homotopy equivalence of path-connected spaces is acyclic. Hence f is a plus construction relative to the trivial subgroup iff f is a weak homotopy equivalence.
hypotheses: X, Y path-connected; for the homotopy-equivalence conclusion, CW complexes.
proofSteps: F = F(f, f x) is path-connected with perfect π₁ (H.3/acyclic-space-perfect-fundamental-group).

In the exact sequence π₂(Y) → π₁(F) → π₁(X) → π₁(Y) (H.2/long-exact-sequence) the last map is injective, so π₁(F) is a quotient of the abelian group π₂(Y); an abelian perfect group is trivial (mathlib Group.IsPerfect).
F is simply connected with H̃_*(F; ℤ) = 0, so π_n(F) = 0 for all n by the Hurewicz theorem (AT stage 8, induction on n).
The exact sequence gives π_n(X) ≅ π_n(Y) for all n at x, hence at every base point by path-connectedness; Whitehead's theorem (AT stage 8) gives a homotopy equivalence for CW complexes.
Converse: the homotopy fibres of a weak equivalence are weakly contractible, hence acyclic by Hurewicz (AT stage 8).
acceptance: Relative to P = ⊥ a plus construction is a weak equivalence (roadmap H.3 test).
Hatcher Example 4.35: S¹ ⊂ (S¹ ∨ S²) ∪_{2t−1} e³ is a π₁-isomorphism and homology isomorphism but not acyclic, so the acyclicity hypothesis cannot be weakened to integral homology.

nodes.title: The plus construction by attaching 2- and 3-cells
nodes.statement: For a connected CW complex X and a perfect normal subgroup P ⊆ π₁(X) there is a relative CW complex X ⊆ X⁺_P obtained by attaching 2-cells along loops representing a generating set of P, which kills exactly P on π₁, and then, writing Y = X ∪ (2-cells), Ỹ for the universal cover of Y (π₁Y = π₁X/P), X_P ⊂ Ỹ for the preimage of X (the connected cover of X with group P) and ẽ_α for a chosen lift of each 2-cell, 3-cells along maps h_α : S² → Y whose lifts S² → Ỹ represent classes mapping to ẽ_α under H₂(Ỹ) → H₂(Ỹ, X_P) ≅ ⊕_α ℤ[π₁X/P]·ẽ_α (such lifts exist because H₁(X_P) = P^{ab} = 0 makes this map onto and π₂(Y) = π₂(Ỹ) ≅ H₂(Ỹ) by Hurewicz). An arbitrary representative of the integral class [e_α] ∈ H₂(Y; ℤ) does not give a plus construction. The resulting inclusion X → X⁺_P is a plus construction relative to P (H.3/plus-fundamental-group, H.3/plus-integral-homology, H.3/plus-is-acyclic). The construction depends on choices; only the homotopy type under X is canonical (H.3/plus-construction-uniqueness).
hypotheses: X connected CW complex; P perfect and normal (for P only perfect, Hatcher kills the normal closure).
proofSteps: Model (Weibel IV Exercise 1.4, with the choice of 3-cells made precise): the 2-cell attachment kills exactly P (H.3/plus-fundamental-group); H₂(Ỹ, X_P) is the free ℤ[π₁X/P]-module on the lifted 2-cells (Hatcher Lemma 4.38 applied to the cover); H₁(X_P) = 0 because P is perfect, so H₂(Ỹ) → H₂(Ỹ, X_P) is onto and the h_α exist by Hurewicz on the simply connected Ỹ (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 8, UniversalCovers stage 2).
Both attachments give a relative CW complex with cells in dimensions 2 and 3 only (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 4 cell attachments).

Hatcher's variant (Proposition 4.40 on the cover X_P glued to the mapping cylinder M_p, §4.2) is homotopy equivalent under X but is not a relative CW complex on X with cells only in dimensions 2 and 3; it is not the model used by the API.
acceptance: Plus construction relative to the trivial subgroup is a homotopy equivalence (roadmap H.3 test).

For the Poincaré homology sphere X = S³/SL₂(F₅), X⁺ is homotopy equivalent to S³ (Weibel IV Exercise 1.1, first part). The composite S³ → X → X⁺ is not an equivalence: it has degree |SL₂(F₅)| = 120 on H₃ (packet source issue StableHomotopyKTheory/E6).
Do not export the local-coefficient isomorphism without H.3/plus-is-acyclic.

Counterexample to the integral-class recipe: X = S¹, P = 1, one 2-cell on the constant loop, Y = S¹ ∨ S², π₂(Y) = ℤ[t, t⁻¹]ι; h = (2t − 1)ι represents [e] ∈ H₂(Y; ℤ) but Y ∪_h e³ is Hatcher Example 4.35, with π₂ ≅ ℤ[1/2], so S¹ → Y ∪_h e³ is not acyclic.

nodes.title: The plus construction is an integral homology isomorphism
nodes.statement: The cell-attachment plus construction X → X⁺_P induces isomorphisms H_*(X; ℤ) → H_*(X⁺_P; ℤ).
hypotheses: X connected CW complex, P perfect normal.
proofSteps: The relative cellular chain complex of (X⁺_P, X) (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 4, relative CW complexes) is ⊕_α ℤe³_α → ⊕_α ℤe²_α with ∂e³_α = e²_α, because h_α maps to e²_α in H₂(Y, X; ℤ) (the augmentation of the lifted class ẽ_α); hence H_*(X⁺_P, X; ℤ) = 0 and the long exact sequence of the pair gives the isomorphism.

This holds for any 3-cell data representing the integral classes [e_α]; integral homology cannot detect the choice made in H.3/plus-construction-by-cell-attachment, which matters only for H.3/plus-is-acyclic (compare Hatcher Prop. 4.40 for P = π₁X).
acceptance: For a perfect group G, BG → BG⁺ is an integral homology isomorphism onto a simply connected space.

nodes.title: The plus construction is acyclic: local-coefficient homology isomorphism
nodes.statement: For the cell-attachment plus construction f : X → X⁺_P and every π₁(X)/P-module M (viewed as a local system on X⁺_P and pulled back to X), f induces isomorphisms H_*(X; M) → H_*(X⁺_P; M). Equivalently (H.3/acyclic-map-homology-criterion) f is acyclic, so it is a plus construction in the sense of H.3/plus-construction-predicate.
hypotheses: X connected CW complex, P perfect normal.
proofSteps: Let π = π₁(X)/P = π₁(X⁺_P) (H.3/plus-fundamental-group). The universal cover X̃⁺ is X_P with the π-translates of the lifted cells attached; its relative cellular chain complex C_*(X̃⁺, X_P) is ⊕_α ℤ[π]ẽ³_α → ⊕_α ℤ[π]ẽ²_α, and by the choice of the h_α (H.3/plus-construction-by-cell-attachment) the boundary is the identity matrix, so H_*(X̃⁺, X_P; ℤ) = 0 (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 4).

The singular chains C_*(X̃⁺, X_P) form a bounded-below acyclic complex of free ℤ[π]-modules, hence a contractible one; tensoring with a π-module M gives C_*(X⁺_P, X; M) (H.3/twisted-homology-via-cover), so H_*(X⁺_P, X; M) = 0.
No source read proves the local-coefficient form for the cell-attachment construction; the argument is packet-authored (packet gap 'Acyclicity of the cell-attachment plus construction').
acceptance: For P = π₁(X) perfect and M = ℤ[π₁X/P] = ℤ this is the integral statement.
For X = BG, f is acyclic and its homotopy fibre is acyclic with π₁ the universal central extension of P (H.3/plus-pi2-universal-central-extension).

nodes.title: Abelian spaces
nodes.statement: A path-connected space X is abelian if π₁(X, x) acts trivially on π_n(X, x) for all n ≥ 1 (Tau Ceti's TauCeti.fundamentalGroupMulAut is trivial); for n = 1 the action is conjugation, so π₁(X) is abelian. The condition is independent of the basepoint. Connected H-spaces are abelian (H.3/hspace-is-abelian).
hypotheses: X path-connected; π_n with the action of Tau Ceti's TauCeti.fundamentalGroupMulAut.
proofSteps: Define IsAbelianSpace X by triviality of the π₁-action on all homotopy groups at one basepoint (Hatcher §4.1, printed p. 342).
Basepoint independence: change of basepoint along a path intertwines the actions (TauCeti.homotopyGroupMulEquivOfPath).
acceptance: Simply connected spaces are abelian.
RP^{2n} is not abelian: π₁ acts by −1 on π_{2n} ≅ ℤ (SSAT p. 38).

sources.excerpt: An important class of abelian spaces is H–spaces, as we show in Example 4A.3.

nodes.title: Connected H-spaces are abelian
nodes.statement: If X is a path-connected H-space (Mathlib's HSpace, unit e), then the action of π₁(X, e) on π_n(X, e) is trivial for every n ≥ 1; in particular X is abelian and π₁(X) is commutative.
hypotheses: X path-connected with an HSpace structure (homotopy unit relative to e).
proofSteps: For a loop γ and f : (Sⁿ, s₀) → (X, e), the map (s, t) ↦ γ(t) · f(s) is a homotopy from f to the action γ·f, using the unit homotopies rel e (Hatcher Example 4A.3, with Proposition 4A.2 identifying the action with free homotopy classes); in Tau Ceti terms the homotopy is a HomotopyAlong γ from f to f, so γ·[f] = [f] by TauCeti.GenLoop.HomotopyAlong.homotopic_transport.
acceptance: Topological groups and loop spaces (Mathlib's HSpace instances for Path x x) are abelian spaces.
BGL(R)⁺ is an H-space and hence abelian (used by H.3/hspace-homology-whitehead).

nodes.title: Eilenberg–Mac Lane spaces K(A, n) as CW complexes
nodes.statement: For n ≥ 1 and a group A (abelian for n ≥ 2) there is a connected CW complex K(A, n) with π_n(K(A, n)) ≅ A and π_i = 0 for i ≠ n, unique up to homotopy equivalence among CW complexes, with based homotopy classes of maps K(A, n) → K(B, n) in bijection with homomorphisms A → B (for n = 1 and B non-abelian, free homotopy classes correspond to homomorphisms modulo conjugation in B); K(A, 1) is BA (H.1/classifying-space-of-group-is-KG1).
hypotheses: n ≥ 1; A abelian when n ≥ 2.
proofSteps: Start from a wedge of n-spheres indexed by generators of A, attach (n+1)-cells along relations to get π_n = A (Hurewicz, Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 8), then kill higher homotopy groups inductively by attaching cells (Hatcher §4.2, 'Eilenberg–MacLane Spaces').

Uniqueness and the bijection on maps: extend maps cell by cell, the obstructions lying in vanishing homotopy groups (Hatcher Proposition 4.30 and Lemma 4.31). Injectivity of the bijection on maps: given based f, g with f_* = g_* on π_n, build a based homotopy on the n-skeleton (a wedge of n-spheres, where f and g agree on each [i_α]) and extend it over the remaining cells of K × I, the obstructions lying in π_{≥ n+1}(K(B, n)) = 0 (Hatcher Lemma 4.7).
acceptance: K(ℤ, 1) ≃ S¹ and K(ℤ/2, 1) ≃ RP^∞.

sources.excerpt: The homotopy type of a CW complex K(G, n) is uniquely deter-mined by G and n .

nodes.title: Relative Hurewicz theorem with trivial π₁-action
nodes.statement: Let (X, A, a₀) be a based pair of path-connected spaces (a based NDR pair in the sense of AT stage 8), (n − 1)-connected with n ≥ 2, such that π₁(A, a₀) acts trivially on π_n(X, A, a₀). Then π_n(X, A, a₀) is abelian, H_i(X, A; ℤ) = 0 for i < n, and the Hurewicz map π_n(X, A, a₀) → H_n(X, A; ℤ) is an isomorphism. A is not assumed simply connected.
hypotheses: π₁(A) acts trivially on π_n(X, A); (X, A) (n − 1)-connected; n ≥ 2.
proofSteps: Reduce to a CW pair by a CW model of (X, A) (AT stage 8 / stage 4 cellular approximation).

Hatcher's proof of Theorem 4.37 (pp. 371–373): Lemma 4.38 (π_n(W, X) is the free ℤ[π₁X]-module on the attached n-cells when π₁X ≅ π₁W, via the universal cover and π_n of coverings) identifies π′_n(X, A) with H_n(X, A); with trivial action π′_n = π_n, and for n = 2 trivial action makes π₂(X, A) abelian.
acceptance: A and X simply connected: the AT stage 8 relative Hurewicz theorem.
Used in Hatcher's proofs of Lemma 4.70 and Proposition 4.74 (H.3/principal-fibration-criterion, H.3/abelian-homology-whitehead).

sources.locator: §4.2, Theorem 4.37 and Lemma 4.38 with proof, printed pp. 371–373 (PDF 380–382)
sources.excerpt: If (X, A) is an (n − 1) connected pair of path-connected spaces with n ≥ 2 and A ≠ ∅ , then h′ : πn′ (X, A, x0 )→Hn (X, A) is an isomorphism and Hi (X, A) = 0 for i < n .
sources.match: Hatcher's general relative Hurewicz theorem, used here in the trivial-action case where π′_n = π_n.

nodes.title: When an inclusion with Eilenberg–Mac Lane fibre is a principal fibration
nodes.statement: Let (X, A) be a CW pair with X and A connected such that the homotopy fibre of A ⊂ X is a K(π, n), n ≥ 1. There is a map k : X → K(π, n+1) whose homotopy fibre receives A by a weak homotopy equivalence compatible with A ⊂ X iff π₁(A) acts trivially on π_{n+1}(X, A) ≅ π.
hypotheses: (X, A) CW pair, X and A connected, hofib(A ⊂ X) ≃ K(π, n), n ≥ 1 (π abelian).
proofSteps: Necessity: in a fibration π₁ of the fibre acts trivially on π_*(E, F) (Hatcher p. 413).

Sufficiency: (X, A) is n-connected with only π_{n+1}(X, A) ≅ π nonzero; relative Hurewicz with trivial action (H.3/relative-hurewicz-trivial-action) gives π_{n+1}(X, A) ≅ H_{n+1}(X, A); absolute Hurewicz on the n-connected X/A gives π_{n+1}(X/A) ≅ H_{n+1}(X/A); attach cells of dimension ≥ n+3 to X/A to get K(π, n+1) and let k be X → X/A → K(π, n+1); the five lemma on the long exact sequences of (X, A) and of the fibration pair shows A → hofib(k) is a weak equivalence (Hatcher Lemma 4.70).
acceptance: A central extension A → S → P: BS → BP has fibre BA = K(A, 1) and S acts trivially on π₂(BP, BS) ≅ A, so BS ≃ hofib(BP → K(A, 2)) (used by H.3/plus-uce-fibration).
RP² ⊂ RP^∞-type examples with non-trivial action are not principal.

sources.excerpt: Then there exists a fi- bration F →E →B and a map (X, A)→(E, F ) inducing weak homotopy equivalences X →E and A→F iff the action of π1 (A) on πn+1 (X, A) is trivial.
sources.match: Hatcher's Lemma 4.70; the proof builds B = K(π, n+1) from X/A.

nodes.title: The Postnikov tower converges
nodes.statement: For a sequence of fibrations ⋯ → X₂ → X₁ the map λ : π_i(lim X_n) → lim π_i(X_n) is surjective, and injective if the maps π_{i+1}(X_n) → π_{i+1}(X_{n−1}) are surjective for large n. Consequently, for a Postnikov tower of fibrations of a connected CW complex X, the map X → lim X_n is a weak homotopy equivalence.
hypotheses: The maps X_n → X_{n−1} are (Hurewicz or Serre) fibrations; X connected CW.
proofSteps: Surjectivity and injectivity of λ by inductive use of homotopy lifting for (Sⁱ, s₀) and (D^{i+1}, Sⁱ) (Hatcher Prop. 4.67).

For a Postnikov tower π_i(X) → π_i(X_n) is an isomorphism for n ≥ i, so the composite π_i(X) → π_i(lim X_n) → lim π_i(X_n) is an isomorphism and the hypotheses of the first part hold (Hatcher Cor. 4.68).
acceptance: A tower with surjective maps on π_{i+1} has no lim¹ term.

sources.locator: §4.3, Proposition 4.67 and Corollary 4.68 with proofs, printed pp. 410–411 (PDF 419–420)
sources.excerpt: For the Postnikov tower of a connected CW complex X the natural map X → lim Xn is a weak homotopy equivalence, so X is a CW approximation to lim Xn .
sources.match: Corollary 4.68 (OCR prints the limit symbol on a separate line).

nodes.title: Cohomology is represented by Eilenberg–Mac Lane spaces
nodes.statement: For a CW complex X, an abelian group G and n ≥ 1, the map T : ⟨X, K(G, n)⟩ → H^n(X; G), [f] ↦ f*(α), with α ∈ H^n(K(G, n); G) the fundamental class (corresponding to id_G under H^n(K(G,n); G) ≅ Hom(H_n K(G,n), G) ≅ Hom(G, G)), is a natural bijection, where ⟨−, −⟩ denotes based homotopy classes and H^n is singular cohomology (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 6). For n ≥ 2 (K(G, n) simply connected) based and free classes coincide (Hatcher p. 394); this is the form used by H.3/obstruction-lifting.
hypotheses: X a CW complex (or of CW homotopy type); n ≥ 1; G abelian.
proofSteps: The functors h^n(X) = ⟨X, K(G, n)⟩ form a reduced cohomology theory on based CW complexes (wedge axiom, exactness from cofibre sequences, suspension iso from ΩK(G, n+1) ≃ K(G, n)) (Hatcher Theorem 4.58, printed p. 397, applied to the Ω-spectrum K(G, n) ≃_w ΩK(G, n+1); proof of Theorem 4.57, p. 402).

A cohomology theory with the same coefficients as H̃^*(−; G) and a natural map is isomorphic to it (uniqueness of cohomology theories on CW complexes, Hatcher Theorem 4.59, printed p. 399, by cellular comparison with Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stages 4 and 6).
acceptance: ⟨X, K(ℤ, 1)⟩ = H¹(X; ℤ) = [X, S¹] (Hatcher §4.3, Exercise 2).
k-invariants of Postnikov towers are classes in H^{n+1}(X_{n−1}; π_n X).

sources.excerpt: There are natural bijections T : hX, K(G, n)i→H n(X; G) for all CW complexes X and all n > 0 , with G any abelian group.
sources.match: Hatcher's Theorem 4.57, proved via Theorem 4.59 on uniqueness of cohomology theories.

nodes.title: Postnikov towers of principal fibrations for abelian spaces
nodes.statement: Every connected CW complex X has a Postnikov tower ⋯ → X_n → X_{n−1} → ⋯ → X_1 with maps X → X_n inducing isomorphisms on π_i for i ≤ n, π_i(X_n) = 0 for i > n, X → lim X_n a weak homotopy equivalence (H.3/postnikov-limit-weak-equivalence), and X_n → X_{n−1} a fibration with fibre K(π_n X, n). The tower can be chosen with each X_n → X_{n−1} a principal fibration, i.e. the homotopy fibre of a map k_n : X_{n−1} → K(π_n X, n+1), iff π₁(X) acts trivially on π_n(X) for all n > 1 (in particular for abelian X). If X is abelian the tower extends by X₀ = point with X₁ → X₀ principal (X₁ ≃ ΩK(π₁X, 2)).
hypotheses: X connected CW complex.
proofSteps: Construct X_n by attaching cells to X to kill π_i for i > n (Hatcher Example 4.16) and convert the maps X_n → X_{n−1} into fibrations with fibre K(π_n X, n) (Hatcher §4.3, p. 410; H.2/mapping-path-space-fibration).

Principality: for n ≥ 2 the action of π₁(X) on π_n(X) is identified with the action of π₁(X_n) on π_{n+1}(X_{n−1}, X_n) (exact sequence of the pair), and H.3/principal-fibration-criterion applies (Hatcher proof of Theorem 4.69, pp. 413–414); conversely a principal fibration has trivial action. For abelian X, X₁ = K(π₁X, 1) ≃ ΩK(π₁X, 2) gives the extra principal stage X₁ → X₀ = ∗ (Hatcher p. 416).
acceptance: For X = K(G, 1) the tower is constant from n = 1.
For RP² the action is nontrivial and no tower of principal fibrations exists.

sources.excerpt: A connected CW complex X has a Postnikov tower of principal fibra-tions iff π1 (X) acts trivially on πn (X) for all n > 1 .
sources.match: Hatcher's Theorem 4.69, after the construction of Postnikov towers.

nodes.title: Obstructions to extending maps through a principal fibration
nodes.statement: Let X_n → X_{n−1} be the principal fibration pulled back from the path fibration over K = K(π_n X, n+1) along k_n, (W, A) a CW pair and W → X_{n−1} a map with a lift A → X_n. The map W ∪ CA → K determines ω_n ∈ H^{n+1}(W ∪ CA; π_n X) ≅ H^{n+1}(W, A; π_n X), and a lift W → X_n extending the given one on A exists iff ω_n = 0.
hypotheses: (W, A) a CW pair; the fibration principal (H.3/postnikov-principal-fibrations).
proofSteps: A lift W → X_n is a null-homotopy of W → X_{n−1} → K extending the given one on A, i.e. an extension of W ∪ CA → K over CW (pullback description of X_n).

Such an extension exists iff W ∪ CA → K is null-homotopic (homotopy extension for (CW, W ∪ CA), Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 4), iff its class ω_n vanishes (H.3/cohomology-representability) (Hatcher Proposition 4.72).
acceptance: If H^{n+1}(W, A; π_n X) = 0 there is no obstruction at stage n.

sources.excerpt: A lift W →Xn extending the given A→Xn exists iff ωn = 0 .
sources.match: Hatcher's Proposition 4.72.

nodes.title: Extending maps into abelian spaces
nodes.statement: If X is a connected abelian CW complex and (W, A) a CW pair with H^{n+1}(W, A; π_n X) = 0 for all n, then every map A → X extends to a map W → X.
hypotheses: X connected abelian CW complex; (W, A) a CW pair.
proofSteps: Lift inductively through the principal Postnikov tower (H.3/postnikov-principal-fibrations), the obstructions vanishing by hypothesis (H.3/obstruction-lifting).

Pass to W → lim X_n and compress to X using the weak equivalence X → lim X_n (H.3/postnikov-limit-weak-equivalence) and the compression lemma (Hatcher Lemma 4.6, Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 8), as in the paragraph before Corollary 4.73.
acceptance: Used with W the mapping cylinder of a homology isomorphism to build a retraction (H.3/abelian-homology-whitehead).

sources.excerpt: If X is a connected abelian CW complex and (W , A) is a CW pair such that H n+1 (W , A; πn X) = 0 for all n , then every map A→X can be extended to a map W →X .
sources.match: Hatcher's Corollary 4.73.

nodes.title: Homology Whitehead theorem for abelian spaces
nodes.statement: If X and Y are connected abelian CW complexes and f : X → Y induces isomorphisms on all integral homology groups, then f is a homotopy equivalence.
hypotheses: X, Y connected abelian CW complexes (or of CW homotopy type).
proofSteps: Replace f by the inclusion of a subcomplex via the mapping cylinder (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 4).

H_*(Y, X) = 0 gives H^{n+1}(Y, X; π_n X) = 0 by universal coefficients (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 6), so the identity of X extends to a retraction Y → X (H.3/abelian-extension-corollary); hence π_n(Y) → π_n(Y, X) is onto and π₁(X) acts trivially on π_n(Y, X).

Relative Hurewicz with trivial π₁-action (H.3/relative-hurewicz-trivial-action; AT stage 8 has only the simply connected case) gives π_n(Y, X) = 0 for all n, so f is a weak equivalence and by Whitehead a homotopy equivalence (Hatcher Proposition 4.74).
acceptance: Simply connected case: Hatcher Corollary 4.33.

The abelian hypothesis cannot be dropped: Hatcher Example 4.35 (printed p. 368): X = (S¹ ∨ Sⁿ) ∪ e^{n+1} attached along 2t − 1 ∈ ℤ[t, t⁻¹] = π_n(S¹ ∨ Sⁿ); S¹ ⊂ X is a homology and π₁-isomorphism with π_n(X) ≅ ℤ[1/2], because π₁ acts nontrivially on π_n.

sources.excerpt: If X and Y are connected abelian CW complexes, then a map f : X →Y inducing isomorphisms on all homology groups is a homotopy equivalence.
sources.match: Hatcher's Proposition 4.74.

nodes.title: Homology isomorphisms between H-spaces are homotopy equivalences
nodes.statement: Let X and Y be path-connected H-spaces of CW homotopy type and f : X → Y a map inducing an isomorphism H_*(X; ℤ) ≅ H_*(Y; ℤ). Then f is a homotopy equivalence. (f need not be an H-map.)
hypotheses: X, Y path-connected H-spaces with the homotopy type of CW complexes.
proofSteps: H-spaces are abelian (H.3/hspace-is-abelian); apply H.3/abelian-homology-whitehead after CW replacement.
Weibel's hint (trivial action of π₁(Y) on the homotopy fibre by [Wh, IV.3.6] and relative Hurewicz) is replaced by this route.
acceptance: BGL(R)⁺ ≃ H whenever BGL(R) → H is an integral homology isomorphism into an H-space (H.3/plus-hspace-recognition).

sources.excerpt: Let X and Y be H-spaces having the homotopy type of a CW complex. If f : X → Y is a map which induces an isomorphism H∗ (X, Z) ∼ = H∗ (Y, Z), show that f is a homotopy equivalence.
sources.match: Weibel's 'standard result' of Exercise 1.3, proved here from Hatcher 4A.3 and 4.74.

nodes.title: Universal property of the plus construction
nodes.statement: Let f : X → Y be a plus construction relative to P of connected CW complexes and g : X → Z a map to a connected abelian CW complex (for instance a connected H-space, H.3/hspace-is-abelian). Then P ⊆ ker(π₁ g) automatically (P is perfect and π₁Z abelian), there is h : Y → Z with h ∘ f ≃ g, and any two such h are freely homotopic; hence the maps h_* on homotopy groups are independent of h. The general case of Weibel IV Theorem 1.5(2) (arbitrary Z) is the packet gap 'Plus-construction universal property for non-abelian targets'.
hypotheses: X, Y connected CW complexes (or of CW homotopy type); Z a connected abelian CW complex.
Uniqueness is up to free homotopy, never literal equality of maps; for abelian Z free and based effects on π_* agree.
proofSteps: Make f cellular and replace it by the inclusion X ⊆ M_f of its mapping cylinder (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 4: cellular approximation, mapping cylinders; M_f ≃ Y rel X). Since f is acyclic it is an integral homology isomorphism (H.3/acyclic-map-homology-criterion with M = ℤ), so H_*(M_f, X; ℤ) = 0 (Hatcher §4.3 Exercise 23, hint).

Existence: the obstruction groups H^{n+1}(M_f, X; π_n Z) vanish by universal coefficients (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 6); extend g over M_f by H.3/abelian-extension-corollary. Uniqueness: apply the same to (M_f × I, M_f × ∂I ∪ X × I), whose relative homology also vanishes.

The non-abelian case is not proved here. A route without twisted obstruction theory (packet-authored, not used): with W = Z ∪_X M_f, van Kampen gives π₁Z ≅ π₁W because g kills P, excision with local coefficients and H.3/acyclic-map-homology-criterion show Z → W is acyclic, so it is a homotopy equivalence by H.3/acyclic-pi1-iso-weak-equivalence.
acceptance: Functoriality of BGL(R)⁺ in R holds only up to homotopy and follows from (2) (Weibel IV 1.1.2).
Lemma 4.4.1 (group completion of group-like H-spaces) uses this with abelian targets.
Do not replace (2) by an assumed structure field.

sources.excerpt: its proof uses topological obstruction theory. Part (1) is proven in Ex. 1.4; an explicit proof may be found in §5 of [Berrick].
sources.match: Shows the universal property is stated with an external proof reference; the abelian-target proof is from Hatcher.

planet.name: Universal property of the plus construction

nodes.title: Uniqueness of the plus construction up to homotopy under X
nodes.statement: If f : X → Y and f′ : X → Y′ are plus constructions relative to P of connected CW complexes and Y′ is abelian (for instance an H-space or simply connected), then the map h : Y → Y′ with h ∘ f ≃ f′ given by H.3/plus-construction-universal-property is a homotopy equivalence. Thus X⁺_P is well defined up to homotopy equivalence under X whenever one model is abelian, but different choices are not equal.
hypotheses: X, Y, Y′ connected CW complexes; Y′ abelian; P perfect normal.
proofSteps: H.3/plus-construction-universal-property gives h : Y → Y′ with h ∘ f ≃ f′.
h is acyclic: for every π₁(Y′)-module M, f and f′ induce isomorphisms on H_*(−; M), hence so does h (H.3/acyclic-map-homology-criterion, both directions).
h induces π₁Y ≅ π₁X/P ≅ π₁Y′, so h is a weak equivalence (H.3/acyclic-pi1-iso-weak-equivalence) and a homotopy equivalence by Whitehead (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 8).
acceptance: Any two models of BGL(R)⁺ are homotopy equivalent (Weibel IV Definition 1.1 remark).

sources.excerpt: In particular, if g is another +–construction relative to P , then the map h in (2) is a homotopy equivalence
sources.match: Weibel's part (3), stated as a consequence of (2).

nodes.title: Functoriality of the plus construction up to homotopy
nodes.statement: Let φ : X → X′ be a map of connected CW complexes and P ⊆ π₁(X), P′ ⊆ π₁(X′) perfect normal subgroups with φ_*(P) ⊆ P′, and X′⁺_{P′} abelian (for instance BGL(R′)⁺, an H-space). Then there is φ⁺ : X⁺_P → X′⁺_{P′}, unique up to homotopy, with φ⁺ ∘ f ≃ f′ ∘ φ; (ψ ∘ φ)⁺ ≃ ψ⁺ ∘ φ⁺ when X″⁺ is abelian, and id⁺ ≃ id. The homotopies are free, so the maps on π₁ commute with the quotient isomorphisms of H.3/plus-construction-predicate only up to conjugation by the track of the base point; for abelian targets there is no ambiguity. Strictly functorial models exist (Weibel IV Constructions 1.9) but the statements here are only up to homotopy.
hypotheses: φ carries the selected perfect subgroup into the selected one; X, X′ connected CW complexes; X′⁺_{P′} abelian.
proofSteps: Apply H.3/plus-construction-universal-property to f′ ∘ φ : X → X′⁺, which kills P since φ_*(P) ⊆ P′ = ker(π₁ f′).
Composition and identities follow from uniqueness up to homotopy.
acceptance: Ring maps R → R′ induce BGL(R)⁺ → BGL(R′)⁺, unique up to homotopy (Weibel IV 1.1.2); for P = E(R) the condition holds because ring maps preserve elementary matrices.

sources.excerpt: a map BGL(R)+ → BGL(R′ )+ , unique up to homotopy, by Theorem 1.5 below
sources.match: Weibel's functoriality up to homotopy, derived from Theorem 1.5.

nodes.title: Recognising plus constructions into H-spaces
nodes.statement: Let X be a connected CW complex whose fundamental group has perfect commutator subgroup P = [π₁X, π₁X] (for example X = BGL(R), P = E(R)), and let g : X → H be a map to a path-connected H-space of CW homotopy type. Then g factors up to homotopy through X → X⁺_P by a map g⁺ whose effect on homotopy groups is independent of the factorisation; if moreover X⁺_P is abelian (for instance an H-space, as BGL(R)⁺ is by Weibel IV Exercise 1.11) and g induces an isomorphism H_*(X; ℤ) ≅ H_*(H; ℤ), then g is acyclic and g⁺ : X⁺_P → H is a homotopy equivalence.
hypotheses: H a path-connected H-space of CW homotopy type; X⁺_P must itself be an H-space for the last clause (true for BGL(R)⁺, Weibel IV Exercise 1.11).
proofSteps: π₁(H) is abelian (H.3/hspace-is-abelian), so P = [π₁X, π₁X] maps trivially; H is abelian, so H.3/plus-construction-universal-property (abelian-target case) gives g⁺, unique up to homotopy, which fixes its effect on π_* (Weibel IV Theorem 1.8).

If g is an integral homology isomorphism, so is g⁺ (H.3/plus-integral-homology); X⁺_P and H are abelian, so g⁺ is a homotopy equivalence (H.3/abelian-homology-whitehead); then g ≃ g⁺ ∘ f is acyclic (homotopy fibres are invariant under homotopy, H.2/homotopy-fibre-transport, and under composition with a homotopy equivalence) (Weibel IV Remark 1.8.1, Exercise 1.3).
acceptance: BGL(F_q)⁺ ≃ the homotopy fibre of ψ^q − 1 on BU, by applying the recognition to Quillen's Brauer-lift map (Weibel IV Theorem 1.12, the use in KTheoryFiniteLocalFields:L.1).
Z × BGL(R)⁺ ≃ the group completion of ⊔ BGL_n(R) (H.4/gl-telescope-plus-comparison).

sources.excerpt: The map i : BGL(R) → BGL(R)+ is universal for maps into H-spaces.
sources.match: Weibel's Theorem 1.8 (proof omitted, citing Gersten) and Remark 1.8.1 (proof indicated in Exercise 1.3), proved here from the abelian obstruction theory.

uses.how: BGL(F_q)⁺ ≃ FΨ^q from an integral homology isomorphism into an H-space (the consumer cites H.3/plus-construction-universal-property for this)

nodes.title: π₂ of a plus construction and universal central extensions
nodes.statement: Let P be a perfect normal subgroup of a group G and f : BG → BG⁺ the plus construction relative to P, with homotopy fibre F(f). Then π₁F(f) is the universal central extension of P and π₂(BG⁺) ≅ H₂(P; ℤ). For G = GL(R), P = E(R) this identifies π₂BGL(R)⁺ with H₂(E(R); ℤ), the kernel of the Steinberg extension.
hypotheses: P perfect normal in G; the recognition theorem for universal central extensions (a central extension X of a perfect group is universal iff H₁(X) = H₂(X) = 0, with kernel H₂(P) by Hopf's formula) is the node K2SymbolsBrauer:T.1/recognition-theorem with the kernel computation K2SymbolsBrauer:T.1:classical/uce-kernel-h2 (RT-AREA-ktheory-1/30).
proofSteps: The homotopy sequence gives π₂(BG) = 0 → π₂(BG⁺) → π₁F(f) → G → G/P → 1, so π₁F(f) is an extension of P by π₂(BG⁺) (H.2/long-exact-sequence).

π₂(BG⁺) is central in π₁F(f): the image of π₂(B) → π₁(F) of a fibre sequence is central (H.2/fibre-sequence-low-degree in its general form: ∂ is equivariant for the conjugation action of π₁(F) and the action of π₁(F) on π₂(BG⁺), which is trivial because F → BG⁺ is null; Hatcher printed p. 413; [Wh, IV.3.5]).
F(f) is acyclic, so π₁F(f) is perfect with H₂ = 0 (H.3/acyclic-space-perfect-fundamental-group).
The recognition theorem (K2SymbolsBrauer:T.1/recognition-theorem) identifies π₁F(f) as the universal central extension of P, whose kernel is H₂(P; ℤ) (Weibel IV Proposition 1.7).
acceptance: K₂(R) = π₂BGL(R)⁺ ≅ H₂(E(R); ℤ) (Weibel IV Corollary 1.7.1).
For P = G perfect, π₂(BG⁺) ≅ H₂(G; ℤ) agrees with Hurewicz on the simply connected BG⁺.
Naturality in R is H.3/plus-pi2-natural (the plus construction is only homotopy functorial).

sources.locator: Proposition 1.7 with proof and Corollary 1.7.1, p. IV.6
sources.excerpt: If F (f ) is the homotopy fiber of f then π1 F (f ) is the universal central extension of P , and π2 (BG+ ) ∼ = H2 (P ; Z).
sources.match: Statement of Proposition 1.7; the proof steps follow Weibel's four-line argument.

planet.name: π₂ of BG⁺ and universal central extensions

nodes.title: Naturality of π₂(BG⁺) ≅ H₂(P; ℤ)
nodes.statement: Let φ : G → G′ be a homomorphism with φ(P) ⊆ P′ for perfect normal subgroups P ⊆ G, P′ ⊆ G′, f : BG → BG⁺ and f′ : BG′ → BG′⁺ plus constructions relative to P and P′, and φ⁺ : BG⁺ → BG′⁺ with a homotopy H : φ⁺ ∘ f ≃ f′ ∘ Bφ (H.3/plus-construction-functoriality). Assume either that H is based or that π₁(BG′⁺) acts trivially on π₂(BG′⁺) (e.g. BG′⁺ an H-space). Then under the isomorphisms π₂(BG⁺) ≅ H₂(P; ℤ) and π₂(BG′⁺) ≅ H₂(P′; ℤ) of H.3/plus-pi2-universal-central-extension, φ⁺_* corresponds to H₂(φ|_P; ℤ).
hypotheses: φ(P) ⊆ P′; H based, or trivial π₁-action on π₂ of the target.
proofSteps: H induces a map of homotopy fibres F(f) → F(f′) compatible with the long exact sequences (H.2/homotopy-fibre-transport, H.2/long-exact-sequence).

On π₁ it is a homomorphism of central extensions π₁F(f) → π₁F(f′) over φ|_P : P → P′; by uniqueness of lifts between universal central extensions (K2SymbolsBrauer:T.1:classical/uce-lift) it is the lift, so on kernels it is H₂(φ|_P; ℤ) (K2SymbolsBrauer:T.1:classical/uce-kernel-h2-natural).
The kernels are π₂(BG⁺) and π₂(BG′⁺) via ∂, and ∂ is natural; with a free homotopy the comparison holds up to the π₁(BG′⁺)-action, trivial by hypothesis.
acceptance: For a ring map R → R′, K₂(R) → K₂(R′) corresponds to H₂(E(R)) → H₂(E(R′)) (requested by K3BlochGroups V.1).

sources.locator: Proposition 1.7 with proof and Corollary 1.7.1, p. IV.6
sources.excerpt: Thus π1 F (f ) is a central extension of P with kernel π2 (BG+ ).
sources.match: The identification whose naturality is proved; the naturality itself is packet-authored, as requested by K3BlochGroups V.1.

nodes.title: BP⁺ is the universal cover of BG⁺
nodes.statement: Let P ⊆ H ⊆ G with P perfect and normal in G, and f : BG → BG⁺ a plus construction relative to P. The covering of BG⁺ with group H/P ⊆ G/P, pulled back along f, is a plus construction of BH (≃ the covering of BG with group H) relative to P; hence BH⁺_P is homotopy equivalent to that covering, compatibly with the maps from BH, and π_n(BH⁺_P) ≅ π_n(BG⁺) for n ≥ 2. For H = P this says BP⁺ is the universal cover of BG⁺. For G = GL(R), P = E(R): BE(R)⁺ is the universal cover of BGL(R)⁺ and K_n(R) ≅ π_n BE(R)⁺ for n ≥ 2; for a commutative ring and H = SL(R) (E(R) is the perfect radical of SL(R) since SL(R)/E(R) = SK₁(R) is abelian), BSL(R)⁺ → BGL(R)⁺ is an isomorphism on π_n for n ≥ 2.
hypotheses: P ⊆ H ⊆ G, P perfect and normal in G.
proofSteps: BH is homotopy equivalent to the covering space of BG with group H (H.1/translation-category-classifying-space, X = G/H); it is the pullback along f of the covering of BG⁺ with group H/P (Weibel IV Exercise 1.8 hint).

The pulled-back covering map has the same homotopy fibres as f (covering maps are fibrations; H.2/homotopy-pullback), so it is acyclic, and its kernel on π₁ is P; the covering of BG⁺ and BH⁺_P are both plus constructions of BH relative to P, and BP⁺ (H = P) is simply connected, so H.3/plus-construction-uniqueness applies (abelian target: for H = P both are simply connected; in general take the covering, whose π₁ = H/P, as source and BH⁺_P abelian, e.g. an H-space).
Covering maps induce isomorphisms on π_n for n ≥ 2 (Tau Ceti IsCoveringMap.homotopyGroupMulEquiv).
acceptance: π₁(BE(R)⁺) = 0 and π₂(BE(R)⁺) ≅ K₂(R).
For P = G this is the identity.

sources.excerpt: Show that BP + is homotopy equivalent to the universal covering space of BG+ . Hence πn (BP + ) ∼ = πn (BG+ ) for all n ≥ 2.
sources.match: Weibel's exercise and its GL/E and SL applications; the proof steps are packet-authored from the hint.

nodes.title: The plus-construction fibration of a universal central extension
nodes.statement: If A → S → P is a universal central extension (S and P perfect), there is a homotopy fibre sequence BA → BS⁺ → BP⁺. Consequently π_n(BS⁺) = 0 for n ≤ 2, π_n(BS⁺) ≅ π_n(BP⁺) for n ≥ 3, and π₃(BP⁺) ≅ H₃(S; ℤ) by Hurewicz. For S = St(R), P = E(R): K_n(R) ≅ π_n BSt(R)⁺ for n ≥ 3 and K₃(R) ≅ H₃(St(R); ℤ).
hypotheses: A → S → P universal central extension; plus constructions relative to the whole perfect groups.
proofSteps: BA → BS → BP is a fibre sequence (H.2/group-extension-fibration). Since A is central, π₁(BS) = S acts trivially on π₂(BP, BS) ≅ π₁(BA) = A, so BS → BP is, up to weak equivalence, the homotopy fibre of a map k : BP → K(A, 2) (H.3/principal-fibration-criterion, n = 1).

K(A, 2) is simply connected, so k factors through BP⁺ (H.3/plus-construction-universal-property). With F′ the homotopy fibre of BP⁺ → K(A, 2), H.3/plus-relative-fibre-comparison over the simply connected base K(A, 2) (E = BP, F = BS) shows BS → F′ is an integral homology isomorphism.

π₁(F′) is a quotient of π₂K(A, 2) = A, hence abelian, and H₁(F′) = H₁(S) = 0, so F′ is simply connected; BS → F′ is then acyclic with kernel S (H.3/acyclic-map-homology-criterion, π₁ = 0 case) and F′ ≃ BS⁺ (H.3/plus-construction-uniqueness). Rotating BS⁺ → BP⁺ → K(A, 2) gives BA ≃ ΩK(A, 2) → BS⁺ → BP⁺ (H.3/eilenberg-maclane-space).

S and P are perfect and H₂(S; ℤ) = 0 (K2SymbolsBrauer:T.1/uce-perfect, K2SymbolsBrauer:T.1:classical/uce-source-superperfect), so π₁(BS⁺) = 0 and π₂(BS⁺) ≅ H₂(S) = 0; Hurewicz (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 8) gives π₃(BS⁺) ≅ H₃(S), and the long exact sequence identifies π_n(BP⁺) for n ≥ 3 (Weibel IV Exercise 1.9).
acceptance: K₃(R) ≅ H₃(St(R); ℤ) (the use in K3BlochGroups:V.1/k3-h3-steinberg).
For the trivial extension of a perfect group with H₂ = 0, BA is a point.

sources.excerpt: Show that there is a homotopy fibration BA → BS + → BP + . Conclude that πn (BS + ) = 0 for n ≤ 2
sources.match: Weibel's exercise and its Steinberg application.

nodes.title: Plus constructions of fibre sequences
nodes.statement: Let F → E →p B be a homotopy fibre sequence of connected CW complexes with B simply connected, P ⊆ π₁(E) a perfect normal subgroup, f : E → E⁺ a plus construction relative to P and p⁺ : E⁺ → B with p⁺ ∘ f ≃ p (H.3/plus-construction-universal-property; B is abelian). Let F′ be the homotopy fibre of p⁺ and F → F′ the map induced by f and the homotopy. Then F → F′ is an integral homology isomorphism. If F′ is simply connected, F → F′ is acyclic with kernel π₁(F) (which is therefore perfect), so F′ ≃ F⁺ under F and F⁺ → E⁺ → B is a homotopy fibre sequence. If F′ is only abelian and F → F⁺ is a plus construction relative to Q = ker(π₁F → π₁F′) with F⁺ abelian, then F⁺ ≃ F′ under F.
hypotheses: B simply connected, so both Serre spectral sequences have constant coefficients; all spaces connected CW complexes.
proofSteps: Compare the Serre spectral sequences of F → E → B and F′ → E⁺ → B over the identity of B (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 5); since E → E⁺ is an integral homology isomorphism, H.3/serre-comparison-fibre gives that F → F′ is one.

If F′ is simply connected, F → F′ is acyclic (H.3/acyclic-map-homology-criterion, π₁ = 0 case) with kernel π₁F, hence a plus construction, and F′ ≃ F⁺ (H.3/plus-construction-uniqueness). If F′ is abelian, the universal property gives F⁺ → F′ under F, an integral homology isomorphism of abelian spaces, hence a homotopy equivalence (H.3/abelian-homology-whitehead).

No source read states the general relative plus construction; the form here is packet-authored around Weibel IV Exercise 1.9 and the roadmap's requirement ('Include the relative construction needed to compare fibres after applying plus'); recorded in the gap 'Relative plus construction'.
acceptance: The universal central extension case BA → BS⁺ → BP⁺ (H.3/plus-uce-fibration).
For a product E = F × B with P ⊆ π₁F the conclusion is (F × B)⁺ ≃ F⁺ × B (Weibel IV Exercise 1.7 for products of groups).

sources.excerpt: Show that there is a homotopy fibration BA → BS + → BP + .
sources.match: The model case of the relative comparison; the general statement is packet-authored.

nodes.title: Serre classes in fibrations with trivial action
nodes.statement: Let C be one of FG (finitely generated abelian groups), T_P (P-torsion) or F_P (finite P-torsion). Let F → X → B be a fibration of path-connected spaces with π₁(B) acting trivially on H_*(F; ℤ). If H_n(F; ℤ) and H_n(B; ℤ) lie in C for all n > 0, so does H_n(X; ℤ); if H_n(F; ℤ) and H_n(X; ℤ) lie in C for all n > 0, so does H_n(B; ℤ).
hypotheses: Trivial monodromy on H_*(F; ℤ); C closed under subgroups, quotients, extensions, ⊗ and Tor (SSAT properties (1), (2)).
proofSteps: Case 1: E²_{p,q} = H_p(B) ⊗ H_q(F) ⊕ Tor(H_{p−1}(B), H_q(F)) ∈ C for (p, q) ≠ (0, 0) (universal coefficients for the untwisted E² page, AT stage 5); by induction on r the pages stay in C, and H_n(X) is filtered with quotients E^∞_{p, n−p} ∈ C.
Case 2: induction on k using the exact sequences 0 → E^{r+1}_{k,0} → E^r_{k,0} → im d_r → 0 (Hatcher SSAT, proof of Lemma 1.9).
acceptance: A product fibration F × B → B satisfies the hypothesis.
Without trivial action the lemma fails: S¹ ∨ S² has finitely generated homology but its universal cover does not (SSAT p. 14).

sources.excerpt: Let F →X →B be a fibration of path-connected spaces, with π1 (B) act- ing trivially on H∗ (F ) . Then if two of F , X , and B have Hn ∈ C for all n > 0 , so does the third.
sources.match: Cases 1 and 2 of the lemma (SSAT omits case 3, which is not needed).

nodes.title: Homology of Eilenberg–Mac Lane spaces lies in the Serre class
nodes.statement: For C one of FG, T_P, F_P and π ∈ C, H_k(K(π, n); ℤ) ∈ C for all k, n > 0.
hypotheses: π abelian in C; n ≥ 1.
proofSteps: Reduce to n = 1 by the path fibration K(π, n−1) → P → K(π, n) (base simply connected for n ≥ 2) and H.3/serre-class-fibration.

n = 1, C = FG or F_P: π is a finite product of cyclic groups; K(G₁ × G₂, 1) = K(G₁, 1) × K(G₂, 1) (Künneth, AT stage 5, or H.3/serre-class-fibration for the product fibration); K(ℤ, 1) ≃ S¹; H_k(K(ℤ/m, 1); ℤ) = H_k(ℤ/m; ℤ) is ℤ/m for odd k and 0 for even k > 0 (H.1/bar-complex-comparison with Mathlib's finite cyclic group homology).
n = 1, C = T_P: π is the filtered union of its finitely generated subgroups G, and H_k(Bπ) = colim H_k(BG) (H.1/filtered-colimit-homology), each in F_P.
acceptance: H_k(K(ℤ/2, 1); ℤ) = H_k(RP^∞; ℤ) is ℤ/2 for odd k, 0 for even k > 0.

sources.excerpt: If π ∈ C then Hk (K(π , n)) ∈ C for all k, n > 0 .
sources.match: Statement and the reduction to n = 1; the cyclic case uses group homology in place of lens spaces.

nodes.title: Serre class theory for abelian spaces
nodes.statement: Let C be one of: finitely generated abelian groups, P-torsion groups, finite P-torsion groups. For a path-connected abelian space X (in particular a connected H-space, such as BGL(R)⁺ or a component of the K-theory space), π_n(X) ∈ C for all n ≥ 1 iff H_n(X; ℤ) ∈ C for all n > 0; and if π_i(X) ∈ C for i < n then the Hurewicz map π_n(X) → H_n(X) is an isomorphism modulo C.
hypotheses: X path-connected and abelian (trivial π₁-action on all π_n, n ≥ 1).
proofSteps: Simply connected case: for the Postnikov tower of X, H_i(X_n) ∈ C for i > 0 by induction on n (H.3/serre-class-fibration, H.3/serre-class-eilenberg-maclane), and H_i(X) ≅ H_i(X_n) for i ≤ n because X_n is X with cells of dimension ≥ n + 2 attached (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 4) (Hatcher SSAT proof of 1.7 and 1.8, p. 16).

Mod-C Hurewicz: the five-term sequence of F_n → X_n → X_{n−1} (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 5) shows H_n(F_n) → H_n(X_n) is an isomorphism mod C, and Hurewicz for the (n−1)-connected F_n = K(π_n X, n) (Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 8) gives Theorem 1.8.

Abelian case: use the tower of principal fibrations (H.3/postnikov-principal-fibrations); in a principal fibration π₁ of the base acts trivially on the homology of the fibre, since the transport maps K(π, n) → K(π, n) are homotopic to the identity (SSAT p. 38). Theorem 1.7 follows by applying 1.8 to the stages.
acceptance: S¹ ∨ S² is not abelian and has π₂ not finitely generated although its homology is (SSAT p. 14): the abelian hypothesis is needed.
If H_*(BGL(R)⁺) is finitely generated in each degree then K_n(R) is finitely generated for n ≥ 1 (the use in ArithmeticKTheory:N.3:finite-generation/quillen-finiteness-criterion).

The same reduction for hermitian K-theory (Calmès et al. Remark 2.3.20): for a number ring O the groups GW^q_n(O; ε) are finitely generated as soon as the integral homology of the components of Ω^∞GW^q(O; ε), which are connected H-spaces, is finitely generated in each degree.

sources.excerpt: This holds also if X is path-connected and abelian, that is, the action of π1 (X) on πn (X) is trivial for all n ≥ 1 .
sources.match: Hatcher's Theorem 1.7 for abelian spaces and the mod-C Hurewicz Theorem 1.8.

sources.excerpt: By Serre class theory, it suffices to show that the ordinary homology groups of the components of Ω∞ GWq (O; 𝜖) are finitely generated.
sources.match: The first step of the remark is this theorem applied to the components, which are connected H-spaces.

nodes.title: Rational homotopy of H-spaces (Cartan–Serre)
nodes.statement: Let X be a path-connected H-space of CW homotopy type with H_n(X; ℚ) finite-dimensional for each n. Then H*(X; ℚ) is a free graded-commutative algebra (polynomial on even and exterior on odd generators) and X_ℚ is a product of Eilenberg–Mac Lane spaces K(ℚ, n_i); π_*(X) ⊗ ℚ has a basis in bijection with the free generators, and the rational Hurewicz map π_n(X) ⊗ ℚ → H_n(X; ℚ) is injective with image the primitive elements of the Hopf algebra H_*(X; ℚ).
hypotheses: X path-connected H-space (hence abelian, H.3/hspace-is-abelian), finite type rational homology. The degree-one factor π₁(X) ⊗ ℚ is included (π₁ abelian).
proofSteps: Hopf–Borel: H*(X; ℚ) is a commutative, associative Hopf algebra of finite type (Künneth, Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 5; cup products, stage 6), hence free graded-commutative (Hatcher AT Theorem 3C.4, printed p. 285).

Cartan–Serre: the product f : X → ∏ K(ℚ, n_i) of the maps given by the generators is a rational homology isomorphism, hence the ℚ-localisation of the abelian space X (SSAT Theorem 1.23, pp. 35–38, P = ∅), using H*(K(ℚ, n); ℚ) = ℚ[x] or Λ[x] (SSAT Proposition 1.20, p. 31, proved with the multiplicative cohomology Serre spectral sequence: packet gap 'Cohomology Serre spectral sequence with products'); so π_*(X) ⊗ ℚ has the stated basis (SSAT Theorem 1.24).

Primitives: Hurewicz images are primitive for the diagonal coproduct (Δ_*[Sⁿ] = [Sⁿ] ⊗ 1 + 1 ⊗ [Sⁿ]); rational Hurewicz is injective because along f it becomes the Hurewicz map of a product of K(ℚ, n)'s, injective factor by factor (Hurewicz in the first nonzero degree, Tau Ceti AlgebraicTopology stage 8 and H.3/hurewicz-degree-one); and dim π_n(X) ⊗ ℚ = number of degree-n generators = dim (QH*)_n = dim Prim(H_*)_n by finite-type duality. Hence the image is exactly the primitives; Milnor–Moore is not needed (packet-authored).
acceptance: π_*(U) ⊗ ℚ is ℚ in odd degrees (SSAT Example 1.25).
RP^{2n} shows the abelian hypothesis is needed (SSAT p. 38).
Borel's computation of K_n(O_F) ⊗ ℚ uses H_*(BGL(O_F)⁺; ℚ) = stable cohomology of arithmetic groups (BorelRegulators:R.3).

sources.locator: Chapter 1, Theorem 1.24 and the paragraph after its proof, pp. 38–39
sources.excerpt: The Cartan-Serre theorem applies to H–spaces whose homology groups are finitely generated, according to Theorem 3C.4 of [AT].
sources.match: Cartan–Serre for abelian spaces and its application to H-spaces.

nodes.title: The core of a symmetric monoidal category is a symmetric monoidal groupoid
nodes.statement: For a symmetric monoidal category (S, □, e), the core Core S (all objects, only isomorphisms) inherits a symmetric monoidal structure: □ restricts to isomorphisms and the unit, associativity and symmetry constraints are isomorphisms. A symmetric monoidal groupoid is a symmetric monoidal category all of whose morphisms are invertible; Core is the right adjoint of the inclusion of symmetric monoidal groupoids into symmetric monoidal categories with strong monoidal functors. Examples: Core of finitely generated projective R-modules under ⊕ (not strict in the sense of Bhatt–Scholze Definition 12.1, i.e. c_{M,M} is the swap, not the identity; this is unrelated to strict associativity), finite sets under ⊔, based free modules F(R) = ⊔_n GL_n(R) under block sum, Pic(R) under ⊗.
hypotheses: S symmetric monoidal (Mathlib MonoidalCategory + SymmetricCategory); direct sum is not assumed strictly associative or strictly commutative.
proofSteps: The tensor product of two isomorphisms is an isomorphism, and the structure isomorphisms of S lie in Core S, so the coherence axioms hold there (Bhatt–Scholze p. 54; Weibel IV Definition 4.1).
Strong monoidal functors S → T restrict to Core.
acceptance: π₀(B Core S) is the commutative monoid of isomorphism classes S^iso.
For projective modules the symmetry c_{M,M} is not the identity when M ≠ 0 (Bhatt–Scholze Example 12.2(i)).

nodes.title: The classifying space of a symmetric monoidal category is a homotopy-commutative H-space
nodes.statement: For a symmetric monoidal category S with countably many morphisms (or with products taken in compactly generated spaces), BS is an H-space with multiplication B(□) ∘ (B(S × S) ≅ BS × BS)⁻¹ and unit the vertex [e]; it is homotopy associative and homotopy commutative, π₀(BS) is the commutative monoid of components and H₀(BS; ℤ) = ℤ[π₀ BS]. If e is initial in S (e.g. S additive), BS is contractible.
hypotheses: The homeomorphism B(S × S) ≅ BS × BS (H.1/classifying-space-prod) needs a finite factor or compactly generated products; for countable CW complexes the ordinary product is already a CW complex, which covers S = F(R) for countable R. In general Mathlib's HSpace must be applied to the compactly generated product (packet gap 'Realisation of products').
proofSteps: The unit isomorphisms e □ s ≅ s ≅ s □ e are natural transformations, hence homotopies (H.1/natural-transformations-adjoints-contractibility), making [e] a two-sided unit up to homotopy rel [e] after the standard modification; associativity and symmetry constraints give the homotopies (Weibel IV §4 opening).
If e is initial, BS is contractible (H.1/contractible-of-initial-or-terminal).

Modify B(□) within its homotopy class so that it is strictly unital at the vertex [e] and the two unit homotopies are relative to [e], as Mathlib's HSpace requires: use the edges of λ_e, ρ_e and the homotopy extension property of the CW pair (BS × BS, BS ∨ BS) (tauceti AlgebraicTopology stage 4).
acceptance: B(Finset under ⊔) is contractible but B(Core) ≃ ⊔ BΣ_n is not (Weibel IV §4 opening and 4.1.1(a)).
For S = Pic(R), B Pic(R) ≃ Pic(R) × B(R^×) (Weibel IV Example 4.1.1(d)).

nodes.title: Quillen's S⁻¹S construction for a symmetric monoidal groupoid
nodes.statement: For a symmetric monoidal groupoid S in which translations Aut(s) → Aut(s □ t) are injective, S⁻¹S has objects pairs (m, n) and morphisms equivalence classes of composites (m₁, m₂) → (s □ m₁, s □ m₂) → (n₁, n₂), two composites being equivalent when an isomorphism α : s ≅ t identifies their second parts. S⁻¹S is symmetric monoidal with (m, n) □ (m′, n′) = (m □ m′, n □ n′), m ↦ (m, e) is monoidal, and K(S) := B(S⁻¹S), K_n(S) := π_n B(S⁻¹S). A strict monoidal functor S → T induces S⁻¹S → T⁻¹T.
hypotheses: Every morphism of S an isomorphism; translations faithful (not needed to define S⁻¹S; it makes each morphism determine s, f, g up to unique isomorphism, which Exercise 4.5 and Theorem 4.8 use).
proofSteps: Define S⁻¹S as ⟨S, S × S⟩ for the diagonal action (H.4/monoidal-action-category), equivalently by Weibel's explicit description (Definition 4.2, Explanation 4.2.1).
The monoidal structure is componentwise (Remark 4.2.2); there is a morphism (e, e) → (m, n) □ (n, m) giving inverses on π₀, not natural (Exercise 4.3).
acceptance: Pic(R) with π₀ already a group gives K₀ = Pic(R), K₁ = R^× and K_n = 0 for n ≥ 2 (Weibel IV Example 4.4.2).
There is no natural transformation 0 ⇒ id □ ι on S⁻¹S (Weibel IV Exercise 4.3): the homotopy inverse is not given by a natural transformation.
Do not use the nerve of all projective-module maps; BP(R) is contractible, only iso P(R) carries the group completion input.
